t: What product sense means for engineers: where it shows up in senior loops, what interviewers score, and a reusable answer structure
sum: Product sense for ML and AI engineers: the four judgements it covers, where senior loops test it, the signals interviewers write down, and a six-step structure (users, goal, metrics, solution, risks, launch) worked end to end with numbers.
prereq: ml16
Offline metrics such as AUC or log loss measure a model on held-out data; the thing a business cares about (retention, revenue, time saved) is measured online, and the two can disagree.
math7
An A/B test randomly splits users into control and treatment; a power calculation tells you how many users you need to detect an effect of a given size.
hd3
A recommendation system design: candidate generation, ranking, and a metrics section that names offline and online measures.
beh6
Ownership and impact stories: how to describe a decision you made, the numbers it moved and what you learned.
why:
Picture a strong engineer in the last round of a senior ML loop. The prompt is "design the recommendations for our short-video app". They draw a clean two-stage system: candidate generation with embeddings, a ranking model with a few hundred features, a feature store, a serving path that hits a 100-millisecond budget. Twenty-five minutes in, the interviewer asks a quiet question: "What is the ranking model optimising, and how would you know the launch was a success?" The candidate says "click-through rate, and offline AUC". The interviewer follows up: "Clicks are up 4% in the experiment, but people who got the new model are 1% less likely to come back next week. Do you ship?" The candidate hesitates, then says "probably yes, clicks are the main metric".

That answer costs the level. Not because the architecture was weak, but because the candidate showed they could build a system without being able to say what it is for or whether it worked. A ranking model that drives clicks while users quietly leave is a well-engineered way of damaging the product. At senior levels, interviewers expect you to catch that before anyone asks.

The same gap shows up in other places. In "how would you add an LLM to this product?" questions, the weak answer jumps to the prompt and the vector database; the strong one asks who the feature is for, what success looks like, what it costs per user and what happens when the model is wrong. In metric questions ("daily active users dropped 10%, what happened?"), the weak answer lists guesses; the strong one has a method. In behavioural rounds, the weak impact story says "we launched X"; the strong one says what moved, by how much, and how they knew it was the launch that moved it.

This lesson defines product sense in terms an engineer can practise. It covers the four judgements it is made of, where senior loops test it, what interviewers actually write on their scorecards, and a six-step structure (users, goal, metrics, solution, risks, launch) that works for most product and metric questions. It ends with a full worked example with numbers, the habits that separate senior answers from mid-level ones, and how the same thinking shows up in real engineering work. The rest of the track goes deep on each step.
primer:
Product sense is the judgement to decide what to build and for whom, define what success means before you build it, choose a solution that fits the problem, anticipate what could go wrong, and decide from evidence whether the thing you built should stay. For an ML or AI engineer it has a sharper edge: a model optimises exactly the objective you give it, so choosing that objective is a product decision that engineers make every day, whether or not they think of it that way.

A useful analogy is a good doctor's consultation. The doctor does not start by prescribing. They first find out who the patient is and what is bothering them (the user and the problem). They decide what "better" would look like for this patient: no pain when walking, not a perfect blood test (the goal). They pick a few measurements that track it, plus a few that must not get worse, such as kidney function while on a drug (metrics and guardrails). Then they choose the least invasive treatment that could work, rest and physiotherapy before surgery (the solution, simplest first). They warn about side effects and what to watch for (risks), and they book a follow-up to check whether it worked (launch and measure).

The analogy breaks in two useful places. First, a doctor has one patient; a product has millions of users whose interests can conflict. A change that delights power users can confuse new ones, and a feed that helps viewers watch more may starve small creators. Much of product judgement is weighing groups against each other. Second, a doctor cannot easily give half of the patients the treatment and half a placebo for every decision, but a software product can. Online experiments let you measure what a change did rather than guess, which is why "how would you measure it" is a central question in every round.

The structure this track uses has six steps, each feeding the next:

The order matters more than the names. Metrics come before the solution because if you pick the solution first, you will unconsciously pick metrics it is good at. The solution step says "simplest first" because the cheapest thing that could work, often a hand-written rule or a popularity list, is both your baseline and sometimes your answer. Risks come before launch because the launch plan must include ways to detect each risk. And the dashed arrow back to the goal is the honest part: most launches teach you something that changes what you aim for next.

A reader who stops here has a correct, simplified picture: product sense means starting from users and a clearly stated goal, measuring the right thing, preferring simple solutions, naming risks, and letting evidence decide. The body explains each piece, how interviewers score it, and how to run the whole structure in a timed round.

One more framing helps. Product questions in interviews come in three shapes, and the same structure handles all of them with a different emphasis. A design question ("build X", "add an LLM to Y") spends most of its time on users, goal and solution. A measurement question ("how would you measure the success of X?") spends most of its time on metrics and launch. A diagnosis question ("metric Z dropped, why?") runs the structure backwards: it starts from a moved metric and works back to which users, which goal and which change explain it. Recognising which shape you have been given in the first minute tells you where to spend your time.

Finally, notice what the structure does not contain: there is no step called "ideas". Ideas appear inside the solution step, after the user, goal and metrics are fixed, and they are judged against those metrics. That ordering is what separates product sense from brainstorming. A candidate who produces ten clever features in the first five minutes has shown creativity; a candidate who produces one feature, explains whom it helps, how its success would be measured and what it would cost, has shown judgement. Interviews for senior engineers reward the second, and so do real launch reviews.
body:
1. The four judgements inside product sense

"Product sense" sounds like a talent. It is more useful to treat it as four separate judgements you can practise and be scored on.

The first is understanding users and their problem. A product serves people with different needs, and the same feature can help one group and hurt another. The judgement is to name the groups that matter (a segment is a subset of users sharing a property such as being new, being on mobile or being a creator rather than a viewer), say which one you are designing for and why, and describe the problem in their words rather than the company's. "Busy parents waste twenty minutes every evening deciding what to cook" is a user problem. "We need more engagement" is a company wish.

The second is defining success. Before building anything you decide what would count as it working, and you express that as metrics. A metric is a number computed from logged behaviour or survey answers, defined precisely enough that two people would compute the same value. The judgement is choosing metrics that move when users genuinely get more value and do not move when they do not. ps2 is entirely about this.

The third is choosing the solution, including whether it should involve machine learning at all. The judgement is to propose the simplest approach that could reach the goal, compare it with more complex ones on expected value and cost, and say what evidence would justify the step up. For ML and AI engineers this includes translating the product goal into a training objective (ps3) and deciding whether an LLM is worth its cost per query (ps8).

The fourth is judging outcomes: reading an experiment, weighing a win on one metric against a loss on another, diagnosing why a number moved, and making a launch call. This is where most real decisions happen, and where engineers who built the system have the most to add, because they know what the logs mean. ps4, ps6 and ps7 cover it.

Interviews rarely announce which judgement they are testing. A system design prompt tests the first three in its opening minutes; a metric-drop question tests the fourth; a "should we build X" question tests all four. Knowing the four lets you notice which one the interviewer is probing when they interrupt.

2. Where it shows up in senior loops

For ML and AI engineers, product judgement is tested in five places, usually without a round being labelled "product sense".

The ML system design round. Most formats for this round, including the widely described format used for ML engineers at large social and ads companies, start with problem framing: what is the business goal, what does the model predict, what label do you train on, which offline metric, which online metric. Candidates who rush through this to reach the architecture are often scored down even when the architecture is good, because the framing determines whether the system is useful. The worked recommendation, search, ads and feed designs in this app (hd3, hd9, hd10, hd11) each have a metrics section for this reason.

"Add AI to this product" questions. A common senior AI-engineer prompt: "We run an email client. How would you add AI summaries?" or "Our support team is overwhelmed; would you build an LLM bot?" These test whether you can decide if the feature is worth it, define success and a launch bar, design for the model being wrong, and estimate cost per user. ps8 to ps10 cover them.

The metric part of every design round. Even a classic infrastructure design, such as a URL shortener or a notification service, ends with "how would you know it is working?" Availability and latency are the engineering answer; a senior answer also says how you would know users are getting value (are shortened links clicked? do notifications get opened and do users not turn them off?).

Product analytics and metric rounds. Some loops, especially for applied scientists and ML engineers working close to products, include a dedicated case: define metrics for a feature, diagnose a drop, or design an experiment. ps4 to ps7 and the cases in ps12 practise these directly.

Behavioural rounds. "Tell me about a project with significant impact" is a product-sense question in disguise. Interviewers listen for whether you chose what to work on for a reason, how you measured impact, and whether you can separate your change's effect from everything else that moved at the same time (beh6 covers story structure).

3. What interviewers write down

Interviewers in structured loops fill in a scorecard with a handful of signals, then write evidence for each. Product questions are scored on roughly the same set everywhere, even if the names differ. Knowing them tells you what to make visible.

SignalWeak evidenceStrong evidence
User focusStarts with the model or the feature listNames segments, picks one with a reason, states their problem concretely
StructureJumps between ideas; hard to followSays the plan up front, signposts each step, summarises decisions
Metric qualityLists many metrics; uses counts that grow with the user baseOne primary metric tied to value, normalised per user, with guardrails and a counter-metric
Trade-off reasoning"It depends" with no resolutionPuts rough numbers on both sides and commits, saying what would change the call
DecisivenessWaits for the interviewer to supply factsStates assumptions with numbers and proceeds; invites correction
Depth on demandStays at slogans when pushedCan go down to how a metric is computed, a power calculation or a cost per query
CommunicationLong monologueChecks in at step boundaries; adapts when redirected

Two things in that table deserve emphasis. First, "normalised per user": a raw count such as total daily sessions goes up whenever more people join, so it cannot tell you whether each user is getting more value. Google's HEART paper makes the same point, recommending averages per user or percentages over raw counts. Second, decisiveness is not the same as overconfidence. "I'd ship, because the primary metric rose 3% and no guardrail moved, but I'd keep a 5% holdout for two months because notification changes often look good early" is decisive and humble at once.

4. The six-step structure, step by step

Step 1, users. Name two to four segments, say who you are designing for, and state their problem in one or two sentences. Useful axes: new versus established users, producers versus consumers (creators and viewers, sellers and buyers, drivers and riders), free versus paying, and heavy versus light users. If the product is a marketplace, say upfront that a change for one side affects the other.

Step 2, goal. One sentence, in user terms, that a non-engineer would agree with: "help busy parents decide what to cook in under two minutes and cook at home more often". The goal is not a metric yet; it is what the metrics are trying to capture. If the company's goal (revenue, growth) differs from the user goal, say how they connect: "if they cook more, they stay subscribed".

Step 3, metrics. One primary metric that best captures the goal and that an experiment can move within a few weeks; two or three guardrail metrics that must not get significantly worse; and, when the primary metric can be gamed, a counter-metric that catches the most likely gaming. Mention a diagnostic metric or two (funnel steps) only if they help explain movements. ps2 covers how to choose these well.

Step 4, solution. Start with the simplest approach that could move the primary metric, often a heuristic or a rule. Then describe the stronger approach (a model, an LLM) and what it would add. Make the comparison concrete: expected improvement, build effort, running cost, risk. For ML features, this is also where you state the training label and objective and how they relate to the primary metric.

Step 5, risks. List the two to four most important ways this could go wrong: for users (wrong or harmful outputs, confusion, privacy), for the business (cost, cannibalising another feature, brand damage) and for measurement (the metric moves for the wrong reason). For each, say how you would detect it: a guardrail, a review sample, an alert.

Step 6, launch. How you would test (usually a randomised experiment, sometimes a staged rollout), how long and on how many users, what result would make you ship, and what you would watch afterwards. Writing the launch criteria before the test starts is the single habit that most protects a team from fooling itself; ps7 covers it.

5. Clarifying questions that earn their time

Open prompts are deliberately vague. Some candidates respond with ten questions; others with none. Both lose time or miss the point. A clarifying question is worth asking only if its answer would change what you propose. Three tests help: does it change who the user is, does it change what success means, or does it rule a solution in or out?

For "add AI meal plans to our recipe app", good questions are "is this for all users or a subscriber feature?" (changes the goal: engagement versus conversion), "are there hard constraints such as allergies or medical diets?" (rules out loose generation without a deterministic filter), and "is the aim to grow, retain or monetise?" (changes the primary metric). Weak questions are ones whose answer you would not use: "what tech stack do you use?" or "how many engineers do we have?" in the first minute.

When the interviewer answers "you decide", that is an invitation to show judgement. Pick, say why in one sentence, and note what would change for the other choice. Then convert everything else into stated assumptions with numbers ("I'll assume four million monthly users, a fifth of them subscribers"). Assumptions are not a weakness; they make your reasoning checkable, and they give the interviewer an easy way to steer you.

6. A worked example, end to end

Prompt: "Panfry is a recipe app (a hypothetical company). Leadership wants AI-generated weekly meal plans. How would you approach it?" Here is a strong answer, compressed, with the numbers made explicit.

Clarify. "Is this a subscriber feature? Any hard dietary constraints?" Interviewer: "Subscriber feature; allergies matter." Assumptions stated aloud: 4 million monthly active users, 900,000 weekly active cooks, 200,000 paying subscribers at $5 a month, and cooking from the app is logged when someone opens step-by-step "cook mode" and reaches the final step.

Users. Three segments: busy parents planning for a family, fitness-focused users tracking protein and calories, and occasional cooks browsing for inspiration. The plan feature targets the first: their problem is decision fatigue and the weekly shop, not a lack of recipes. Fitness users are a good second segment later; occasional cooks are unlikely to plan a week.

Goal. "Help subscribers who cook for a household decide the week's meals in a couple of minutes, so they cook from Panfry more often and stay subscribed."

Metrics. The primary metric is completed cooking sessions per weekly active subscriber, because it measures the value (cooking happened), it is per user (not inflated by growth), and it should respond within weeks. Today's assumed value is 1.6 sessions per week with a standard deviation of 1.9. Guardrails: subscription cancellation rate, allergy and complaint reports per thousand plans, plan-generation latency at the 95th percentile, and cost per plan. Counter-metric: plans generated but never cooked from, which would rise if a pushy prompt inflated plan creation without value. Diagnostic: the funnel from "open planner" to "plan accepted" to "at least one planned recipe cooked".

Solution. Baseline first: a rule-based planner that picks seven highly rated recipes matching the user's saved diet tags, avoids repeats from the last two weeks and balances cooking time across weekdays. It costs nothing per plan and can ship in two weeks. The AI version uses an LLM to take free-text preferences ("kids hate mushrooms, Tuesday is football night, use up the spinach") and assemble a plan from the existing recipe catalogue, never inventing recipes. Allergens are filtered by a deterministic check against recipe ingredient data after the model proposes a plan, because a model's "I avoided peanuts" is not a guarantee. The question the experiment must answer is whether the LLM version beats the rule-based one by enough to pay for itself.

Cost. Assume a plan request uses about 2,500 input tokens (preferences plus a shortlist of candidate recipes) and 1,200 output tokens. At October 2026 list prices for a small model (Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens), that is 2,500 × $1/1M + 1,200 × $5/1M = $0.0025 + $0.006 = $0.0085 per plan. If 300,000 subscribers each generate one plan a week, that is $2,550 a week, about $133,000 a year. At $60 a year per subscriber, the feature pays for its model costs if it keeps about 133,000 / 60 ≈ 2,200 extra subscribers a year, about 1.1% of the 200,000 base. That is a plausible bar, which makes the idea worth testing; if the arithmetic had needed 20% of subscribers, the answer would be to start with the rule-based planner. (Prices move fast: the newer Claude Haiku 5.5 lists a tenth of Haiku 4.5's price for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, which would cut the bill to about $13,000 a year and make the cost bar almost irrelevant; the question would then be whether the cheaper model's plans are good enough, which is ps8's subject.)

Risks. Allergen mistakes (detected by the deterministic filter and by allergy reports, which are a guardrail with a hard threshold of zero confirmed incidents); plans users do not cook from (the counter-metric); cost growing if users regenerate plans repeatedly (cap regenerations, watch cost per subscriber); and the novelty of a new feature inflating early usage (watch the effect week by week, ps6).

Launch. A randomised experiment among subscribers with three arms: control (no planner), rule-based planner and LLM planner. To detect a 3% relative lift on a mean of 1.6 (δ = 0.048) with standard deviation 1.9, the usual approximation for 80% power at 5% significance (math7) gives about n = 16σ²/δ² = 16 × 3.61 / 0.0023 ≈ 25,000 subscribers per arm. With 200,000 subscribers, 25,000 per arm is affordable, and the test runs three weeks so it covers several weekly cycles. Launch criteria, written before the test: ship the LLM planner if it beats the rule-based planner on the primary metric by at least 3% with no guardrail regression and zero confirmed allergen incidents; otherwise ship the rule-based planner if it beats control.

Summary. "Target households, measure cooking not clicking, test a cheap rule-based planner against the LLM one, and let the LLM earn its $133,000 a year."

7. Communicating while you think

Structure is only visible if you say it. Start by announcing the plan: "I'll spend a couple of minutes on who this is for and what success means, then the solution, then risks and how we'd launch." Signpost transitions ("that's my metric set; now the solution"). At the end of each step, summarise the decision in one sentence. When the interviewer interrupts, treat it as information: an interruption usually means "go deeper here" or "you are off track", and either way the right response is to follow it.

Think out loud, but in finished thoughts. "Hmm, maybe clicks, or maybe time spent, or maybe…" is hard to score. "Two candidates for the primary metric: clicks, which respond fast but can be gamed by thumbnails, and cooked sessions, which are closer to value; I'll take cooked sessions" shows the same thinking and a decision.

8. How the rest of this track builds on this

Each of the later topics deepens one step. ps2 turns goals into good metrics; ps3 turns product metrics into what a model actually optimises; ps4 diagnoses metric changes; ps5 covers funnels, cohorts and retention, the vocabulary of growth; ps6 and ps7 cover designing experiments as product decisions and making the launch call; ps8 to ps10 apply all of it to ML and LLM features (whether to build, how to design, how to measure); ps11 covers sizing and prioritising; ps12 runs five full timed cases in the structure introduced here. The statistics behind experiments live in math6, math7 and in10; this track uses them without re-deriving them.
deep:
Metrics are contracts between teams

At a company of any size, a metric is not just a measurement; it is an agreement about what counts as success, and teams organise their work around it. If the recommendations team is measured on watch time and the creator team on uploads, each will make choices that look good on its own metric and may hurt the other's. A senior engineer notices when the metric they are given conflicts with a neighbouring team's, and raises it before the conflict becomes a launch-review argument. In interviews, saying "I'd check this doesn't conflict with what the creator team is measured on" signals that you have worked in real organisations.

Dashboard metrics versus decision metrics

A company tracks hundreds of metrics on dashboards to monitor health. Only a few are used to make launch decisions. The difference matters: a dashboard metric can be noisy, lagging or hard to attribute, because it is for spotting trends; a decision metric must be sensitive enough to move in an experiment's duration, attributable to the change being tested, and agreed in advance. Many weak answers name a company-level dashboard metric (monthly active users, revenue) as the launch criterion for a small feature. The feature cannot plausibly move it enough to detect within weeks, so the experiment would come back flat whatever the feature did. The senior move is to pick a decision metric that the feature can move and to explain how it connects to the company-level metric.

Reframing the prompt, politely

Sometimes the prompt contains a bad assumption: "how do we increase time spent in our meditation app?" (most meditation users want a short, effective session, not more time). Strong candidates name the tension and propose a better goal ("sessions completed per week and a self-reported calm score"), while still answering the question asked. The skill is doing this without lecturing: acknowledge the business reason behind the original goal, show how the reframed goal serves it better in the long run, and let the interviewer choose. Interviewers often plant such a flaw deliberately to see whether you notice it.

Second-order effects and ecosystems

Many products are ecosystems: viewers and creators, riders and drivers, buyers and sellers, readers and advertisers. A change that helps one side shifts behaviour on the other, which shifts the first side's experience again weeks later. A feed change that favours already-popular videos may raise viewer watch time this month and reduce uploads from small creators over the next quarter, which narrows what viewers can watch next year. Senior answers name the other side of the ecosystem, pick a guardrail for it, and acknowledge that a standard short experiment measures only the first-order effect (ps6 covers designs for the rest).

Short-term versus long-term

Experiments typically run for a few weeks, but the business cares about months and years. Some changes win short-term and lose long-term: more notifications raise opens this week and raise disabling of notifications over months; more ads raise revenue today and reduce usage later. Google's Rules of Machine Learning puts it directly in Rule 39: launch decisions are a proxy for long-term product goals. Senior answers say which direction the long-term effect is likely to go for this specific change, and propose a holdout (a small group kept on the old experience for months) when the risk is real.

When data cannot decide

Some decisions cannot be tested well: a change with network effects across the whole product, a brand-level change, or something with small samples (an enterprise product with 300 customers). Other decisions are cheap to reverse and should simply be made quickly. Strong candidates distinguish these: for reversible, low-cost changes they decide fast and monitor; for irreversible or high-stakes ones they invest in better evidence (a longer test, a staged rollout, user research). Saying "this is a two-way door, so I'd ship behind a flag and watch the guardrails" is product judgement too.

Twyman's law and scepticism about your own wins

Twyman's law is the experimenter's rule of thumb that any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong. In practice, a result far better than expected is more likely to come from a bug (logging double-counting, a broken control, bots in one arm) than from a breakthrough. The Bing ad-headline experiment triggered exactly such an alert: the treatment produced revenue so high that an automated "too good to be true" check fired, and the team investigated before believing it. Here the result was real. The habit is what matters: a senior engineer's first reaction to a huge win is to check the data, and to say so in the interview.

What changes for AI and LLM features

Product judgement for features built on a large language model (LLM, a model trained on large amounts of text that generates text in response to a prompt) has three extra dimensions that classic features lack. First, the output is variable and sometimes wrong, so "how good is it?" is a distribution rather than a yes or no: the feature might be excellent 90% of the time and embarrassing 2% of the time, and the product design has to decide what the user sees in that 2% (ps9). Second, every use has a marginal cost. A classic feature costs roughly the same whether 1,000 or 1,000,000 people use it; an LLM feature's bill scales with usage, so success can be expensive, and cost per active user becomes a guardrail (ps8). Third, the offline evaluation of quality and the online measure of value are further apart than usual: a summary can score well on a quality rubric and still not save anyone time (ps10).

In interviews, a candidate who raises these three points unprompted, with a rough number for each (an error rate the product can tolerate, a cost per user, and a plan to measure value online rather than only quality offline), is showing exactly the senior AI-engineer judgement the question was written to find.

Depth on demand

Interviewers test whether your product reasoning rests on real understanding by drilling down: "how exactly is 'cooked session' logged?", "what's the denominator?", "how many users do you need?", "what does a plan cost?". A candidate who can go from "help families cook more" down to an event definition, a power calculation and a cost per request in two minutes is showing the full range a senior role needs. Practise this deliberately: for every metric you propose, be ready to define its numerator, denominator, time window and logging source.
prod:
Where product sense lives in real engineering work

Outside interviews, product judgement shows up as artefacts and rituals. A design document for an ML feature has a "goals and non-goals" section and a "success metrics" section; reviewers push back when the success metric is missing or is a model metric only. A launch review examines the experiment results against criteria agreed before the experiment ran. Metric owners, a named team or person for each important metric, maintain its definition, so that "weekly active user" means the same thing in every dashboard. Post-launch reviews a few months later check whether the effect lasted. Engineers who want senior scope take part in all of these, not just the build.

Characteristic failure modes

Shipping without instrumentation. The feature launches, and only then does someone ask how to measure it, discovering that the key event was never logged. Rule 2 of Google's Rules of Machine Learning, "first, design and implement metrics", exists because this is common. The symptom is a launch review where every chart starts on launch day, so there is no before-and-after comparison.

Choosing the metric after seeing the data. A team runs an experiment, looks at forty metrics, finds three that improved, and declares success on those. With forty metrics and a 5% false-positive rate, about two would look significant by chance alone. The fix is pre-registered launch criteria (ps7).

Local optimisation. A team improves its own metric at another team's expense: a notifications team raises opens by sending more, the app-store rating falls, and the growth team pays for it. The symptom is a company-level metric drifting down while every team reports wins. Guardrails owned by other teams are the remedy.

Average hides the story. An effect that is positive overall but strongly negative for new users can quietly damage growth. Segment checks for the segments that matter (new users, the main platforms, the largest countries) belong in every launch review, interpreted with care (ps4 and ps7).

Mistaking model metrics for product metrics. An ML team reports a 3-point AUC gain as the outcome. Nobody checks that users benefited. Offline metrics are necessary for iterating on models, but the launch decision belongs to online product metrics (ml16).

A real case: the Bing ad headline

Ron Kohavi and Stefan Thomke describe in Harvard Business Review (2017) how, in 2012, a Microsoft employee working on Bing proposed changing the way ad headlines were displayed. It would take an engineer only a few days, but it was one of hundreds of ideas, the program managers judged it low priority, and it sat for more than six months. An engineer who saw how cheap it was finally ran an A/B test. Within hours, revenue in the treatment was so high that it triggered a "too good to be true" alert, which usually signals a bug. Analysis showed the change had increased revenue by 12%, which on an annual basis came to more than $100 million in the United States alone, without hurting key user-experience metrics. The article calls it the best revenue-generating idea in Bing's history.

Three lessons from this case carry through the whole track. First, experienced people are poor at predicting which ideas will matter, so a cheap way to test ideas is worth more than confident prioritisation. Second, the result was trusted because the team had both a guardrail set ("without hurting key user-experience metrics") and a habit of distrusting surprising wins. Third, the success criterion was clear in advance: revenue per search was the goal, and user-experience metrics were the guardrails. Without those, a 12% revenue jump could just as easily have been a change that annoyed users into clicking ads, which is exactly the trap ps2 examines.

Signals that a team has weak product judgement

You can often spot it from the outside: dashboards dominated by raw counts that rise with growth; launches justified by "users loved it in the demo"; experiment write-ups with no pre-stated criteria; arguments in launch reviews about what a metric means; and no one able to say what the model's label is a proxy for. In an interview, describing one of these from your own experience, and what you changed, is a strong behavioural answer.
myths: Product sense is a product manager's skill; engineers are judged on architecture and code.

Senior engineering loops test it directly. An ML system design answer that never says what the model should optimise, or how anyone will know the launch worked, is incomplete however good the architecture is. Senior engineers are expected to push back on a bad objective, size an opportunity before building, and own whether their system moved the outcome it was built for. The engineer is often the only person in the room who knows what the model can actually measure and predict.
Good product sense means having great feature ideas.

Ideas are the cheapest part. Interviewers score whether you understand who the users are, define success before building, pick metrics that cannot be gamed easily, weigh trade-offs with numbers, and make a decision you can defend. A modest idea with a sharp success definition and a credible launch plan beats a brilliant idea with no way to tell whether it worked.
A structured answer means reciting a framework.

A framework is a checklist to stop you forgetting steps, not a script. Interviewers mark down candidates who march through six headings mechanically while ignoring what the interviewer is steering towards. Use the structure to organise your thinking, adapt the time per step to the question, and say why you are skipping a step when it does not apply.
The best answer is the one with the most metrics.

A list of fifteen metrics signals that you cannot decide what matters. Strong answers name one primary metric, two or three guardrails and a few diagnostic metrics, and explain why each is there and what decision it drives.
If the data says ship, you ship; judgement only matters when there is no data.

Data answers the question you measured, over the window you measured it. Judgement decides which question to measure, whether a short-term win could be a long-term loss, whether a result is too good to be true, and what to do when the primary metric and a guardrail disagree. The best experimenters are sceptical of their own wins.
lab:
Goal: practise the six-step structure under time pressure and check your own answer against the signals interviewers score. About 20 minutes; Python 3.12 standard library only.

  1. Pick a prompt: "add AI-written summaries to a podcast app", "a food-delivery app wants to reduce late deliveries", or "a language-learning app wants more paying users".
  2. Set a 12-minute timer and write your answer in a plain text file answer.txt, using six headings: USERS, GOAL, METRICS, SOLUTION, RISKS, LAUNCH.
  3. Save this checker as grade.py and run python grade.py answer.txt:
import re, sys
text = open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8").read()
heads = ["USERS", "GOAL", "METRICS", "SOLUTION", "RISKS", "LAUNCH"]
parts = re.split(r"^(USERS|GOAL|METRICS|SOLUTION|RISKS|LAUNCH)\s*$", text, flags=re.M)
sections = {parts[i]: parts[i + 1] for i in range(1, len(parts) - 1, 2)}
for h in heads:
    body = sections.get(h, "")
    nums = re.findall(r"\d[\d,.]*%?", body)
    print(f"{h:9} words={len(body.split()):4} numbers={len(nums)}")
m = sections.get("METRICS", "").lower()
print("primary named:  ", "primary" in m)
print("guardrail named:", "guardrail" in m)
print("per-user metric:", bool(re.search(r"per (user|active|subscriber)", m)))
print("launch bar:     ", bool(re.search(r"ship|launch if|criteria", sections.get("LAUNCH", "").lower())))

What to look for: every section present; at least one number in GOAL or METRICS, SOLUTION (a cost or effort) and LAUNCH (a sample size, duration or threshold); a primary metric that is per user; guardrails named; and a launch rule written as a condition. The script is deliberately crude: keyword checks cannot judge quality. Re-read the METRICS section and ask, for each metric, "what decision does this drive?" Delete any metric you cannot answer for. Then redo the same prompt in 8 minutes and compare.
recap: Product sense for an engineer is the judgement that links users, business goals and the system you build: what to build, how you will know it worked, and what to do when the number moves.

It shows up in ML system design rounds (problem framing and metrics), in questions about adding an LLM to a product, in the metric section of every design round, and in behavioural stories about impact.
Interviewers write down a small set of signals: user focus, structured thinking, quality of metrics, trade-off reasoning with numbers, decisiveness under stated assumptions, and clear communication.
A reusable answer structure is users, goal, metrics, solution, risks, launch; it is a checklist to adapt, not a script to recite.
Clarifying questions should change your answer; ask the two or three that do, state assumptions for the rest, and move on.
Every metric you name should map to a decision: the primary metric decides launch, guardrails can block it, and diagnostic metrics explain why things moved.
Putting rough numbers on users, effect sizes, sample sizes and cost per user turns opinions into a decision someone can check.
Start with the simplest solution that could work, often a heuristic, and say what evidence would justify something more complex.

The Bing ad-headline experiment (a shelved idea that raised revenue 12% once tested) is the standard reminder that intuition about value is unreliable, which is why success criteria and experiments matter.
glossary: A/B test
A randomised experiment in which users are split at random between the current product (control) and a changed version (treatment), so that differences in outcomes can be attributed to the change.
AUC
Area under the ROC curve: the probability that a model scores a random positive example above a random negative one; an offline ranking-quality metric (ml7).
Baseline
The simplest reasonable solution or the current value of a metric, against which any proposal is compared.
Clarifying question
A question asked at the start of an open-ended prompt to pin down scope, users or constraints; a good one changes the answer you would give.
Counter-metric
A metric chosen to catch the most likely way a primary metric could be gamed or improved at someone's expense, such as unsubscribes alongside notification clicks.
Diagnostic metric
A metric watched to explain why the primary metric moved (for example, a funnel step), not used to decide the launch.
Guardrail metric
A metric that is not the goal but must not get significantly worse, such as latency, crash rate or complaint rate; a guardrail breach can block a launch.
HEART
Google's framework of user-experience metric categories: Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention and Task success (Rodden et al., CHI 2010).
HiPPO
Highest Paid Person's Opinion: decisions made by seniority rather than evidence; a term popularised in the online-experimentation community.
Launch criteria
Conditions, written before an experiment starts, that decide whether a change ships: which metric must move, by how much, and which guardrails must hold.
LLM
Large language model: a model trained on large amounts of text that generates text in response to a prompt; each use has a token cost.
ML
Machine learning: building systems that learn patterns from data rather than following hand-written rules.
North-star metric
The single metric a team treats as the best measurable summary of the value its product delivers to users, used to align many smaller decisions.
OEC
Overall Evaluation Criterion: the metric, or small weighted combination of metrics, that an experiment is designed to improve and that decides success.
Offline metric
A measure of a model computed on stored data without users in the loop, such as AUC, precision or log loss.
Online metric
A measure computed from real user behaviour after a change is live, such as retention, conversion or time to complete a task.
Opportunity sizing
A rough estimate of the most a change could be worth, made before building it, usually reach multiplied by effect multiplied by value per unit.
Power calculation
A calculation of how many users or how long an experiment needs to detect an effect of a given size with a given probability.
Product sense
The judgement to decide what to build for whom, define what success means, choose a solution, anticipate risks and make launch decisions from evidence.
Proxy metric
A measurable stand-in for something you care about but cannot measure directly or quickly, such as clicks standing in for satisfaction.
Segment
A subset of users defined by a shared property (country, platform, new versus returning) used to check whether an effect differs between groups.
Twyman's law
The rule of thumb that any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong; a surprisingly large result should be checked for bugs before it is believed.
drill:
Framing drill (8 minutes)

Tunely, a hypothetical music-streaming app with 30 million monthly users, wants to add an "AI DJ" that talks between songs, introducing tracks and explaining why they were picked. The interviewer asks: "How would you decide whether to build this, and how would you know it worked?" Answer using the six steps, with at least three numbers.

Answer

Users. Lean-back listeners who use radio-style stations and do not want to choose songs (assume 30% of monthly users); active playlist curators (who will mostly ignore a DJ); and new users who have not yet shown taste, for whom explanations might speed up discovery. Target lean-back listeners first.

Goal. "Make lean-back listening feel personal enough that users listen longer per session and discover artists they go on to save."

Metrics. Primary: listening minutes per weekly active lean-back user, because the DJ's value shows up as longer, more satisfying sessions. Counter-metric: skip rate in the first 10 seconds after a DJ segment, and "turn off DJ" rate, because talking can annoy. Guardrails: next-week return rate, premium cancellations, and cost per listening hour. Diagnostic: new artists saved per user, which tests the discovery claim.

Solution. Baseline: templated, pre-recorded intros using metadata ("next up, a 2019 track from an artist you saved"). AI version: an LLM writes short scripts from listening history and track metadata, converted to speech. Cost estimate: one 60-word segment every 4 songs is about 4 segments an hour; if each script costs about $0.001 in model tokens and speech synthesis costs about $0.004, that is about $0.02 per listening hour. With 9 million lean-back users listening 5 hours a week, that is about $900,000 a week, a serious cost to justify, so the experiment must show a meaningful lift or the segments must be cached and reused across users.

Risks. Annoyance (counter-metrics), factual errors about artists (sample review, a source of truth for facts), cost (cap segments per hour), and novelty (track the effect week by week).

Launch. A three-arm test (control, templated, AI) for four weeks among lean-back users. Ship the AI DJ only if it beats templated intros on listening minutes by a pre-agreed margin large enough to pay for its cost, with no increase in DJ-off rate beyond a threshold and no drop in next-week return rate.

The strong signal here is the cost estimate changing the plan: once you see roughly $900,000 a week, you either need a large lift or a cheaper design, and you say so.
qa: E
What does product sense mean for an ML or AI engineer, as opposed to a product manager?

It is the judgement that connects users, business goals and the system you build: deciding what is worth building, defining how you will know it worked, and deciding what to do when the numbers move. A PM owns the roadmap, but the engineer usually owns the objective the model optimises, the instrumentation and the honest reading of results. In a senior loop it shows up as framing the problem before designing, choosing metrics that match the goal, and making a launch call with trade-offs stated.

Follow-up: Where does an engineer's product sense matter most day to day? — In choosing the training label and objective, because a model optimises exactly what you give it, and in the launch review, where the engineer often knows best why a metric moved.
E
Walk me through the structure you use for an open-ended product question.

Users, goal, metrics, solution, risks, launch. I start by naming the user segments and the problem they have, state the goal in one sentence, pick one primary metric plus guardrails, propose the simplest solution that could work and what would justify more, list the main risks and how I would detect them, and finish with how I would launch and what result would make me ship. I adapt the time per step to what the interviewer cares about rather than reciting all six equally.
E
Why should every metric you name be tied to a decision?

Because a metric that changes no decision is noise on a dashboard and makes your answer look unfocused. The primary metric decides whether to ship, guardrails can veto a ship, and diagnostic metrics explain movements. If I cannot say what I would do differently when a metric moves, I drop it from the answer.
E
What is a guardrail metric? Give an example.

A metric that is not the goal but must not get significantly worse. For a recommendation change the goal might be weekly active days, while page latency, crash rate and the rate of 'not interested' clicks are guardrails. A large enough guardrail regression blocks the launch even if the goal metric improves.
M
An interviewer says: 'We want to add AI-generated meal plans to our recipe app.' How do you open?

I ask two or three questions that change the answer: who is the plan for (busy families versus fitness users), whether this is free or part of a subscription, and whether there are hard constraints such as allergies. Then I state assumptions for the rest out loud and give the goal in one sentence, for example 'help subscribers cook at home more often with less planning effort'. That gives me a primary metric (cooking sessions completed per weekly active user) before I talk about models.
Follow-up: What if the interviewer says 'you decide'? — Then I pick the segment where the problem is sharpest and the data is richest, say why, and note how the answer would change for the others.
M
How do you avoid spending the whole interview on clarifying questions?

I ask only questions whose answers would change my design, cap it at a couple of minutes, and convert the rest into stated assumptions with numbers: 'I'll assume 4 million monthly users and that the plan is a subscriber feature.' Assumptions keep the conversation moving and give the interviewer an easy way to redirect me.
M
Why put numbers into a product answer when the interviewer gave you none?

Numbers turn opinions into something checkable. Saying '300,000 users might generate a plan weekly at about a cent each, so roughly $130,000 a year, which needs about 2,200 extra retained subscribers to pay back' lets the interviewer see whether the idea is worth building and how I reason. Rough, clearly labelled assumptions are fine; the point is the reasoning chain, not precision.
M
How would you know an AI meal-plan feature worked?

Define it before launch: the primary metric is cooking sessions completed per weekly active user, measured in a randomised experiment for at least two to three weekly cycles. Guardrails are subscription cancellations, complaint and allergy-report rate, latency and cost per plan. I would ship if the primary metric rises by at least the pre-agreed minimum (say 3%) with no guardrail regression, and I would keep a small holdout to check the effect lasts.

Follow-up: Why not use 'plans generated' as the metric? — Because it measures use of the feature, not value; people can generate plans and never cook from them, and a pushy prompt to generate plans would inflate it.
M
What signals do interviewers write down in a product or metrics question?

User focus (do you start from who has the problem), structure (can they follow you), metric quality (is the metric attributable, sensitive and hard to game), trade-off reasoning (do you weigh costs with numbers), decisiveness (do you commit under stated assumptions) and communication. Depth on demand matters too: when pushed, can you go from strategy down to how the metric is computed.
M
Tell me about the Bing ad-headline experiment and why it matters for product judgement.

In 2012 a Bing employee proposed changing how ad headlines were displayed; it was cheap to build but judged low priority and sat for more than six months. When an engineer finally tested it, revenue rose 12%, worth over $100 million a year in the US, without hurting user-experience metrics, according to Kohavi and Thomke in Harvard Business Review. It shows that experienced people are bad at predicting value, which is why you define success criteria and test, and why a 'too good to be true' alert was checked before it was believed.
H
The interviewer says the goal is 'engagement'. How do you push back without being difficult?

I agree engagement matters and then ask what kind: engagement can rise because users get value or because the product wastes their time or confuses them, as Google's HEART paper notes about page views. I propose a version tied to value, such as 'days per week a user completes the core task', and pair it with a counter-metric such as regret surveys or unsubscribes. Framing it as making the metric harder to fool keeps it collaborative.

Follow-up: And if they insist on raw time spent? — I would accept it as the primary metric but insist on guardrails for satisfaction and long-term retention, and on a long-running holdout, because short-term time spent can trade against long-term retention.
H
How would you structure a 45-minute ML system design round so the product parts don't crowd out the technical parts?

Roughly five to seven minutes on users, goal and metrics, including turning the product metric into a training objective, then the bulk on data, model and serving, then five minutes on risks, evaluation and launch. The product framing is short but it shapes everything after: the label, the offline metric and the online experiment all follow from it. I tell the interviewer my plan up front so they can redirect.
H
You built a model that improved offline AUC by 2 points, and the online experiment shows no change in the primary metric. What do you do?

First check the experiment is valid (sample ratio, logging, exposure), then whether the offline gain is in the part of the distribution that matters (for example the top few ranked slots), whether the label is a weak proxy for the online goal, and whether the experiment had power to see the effect a 2-point gain could produce. If all hold, the honest conclusion is that this offline metric does not predict this online goal well, and the next investment is a better label or offline metric, not another model.
Follow-up: Would you ship it anyway? — Only if it is cheaper to serve or simpler to maintain and no guardrail moved; otherwise extra complexity with no measured benefit is a cost.
refs: Kohavi & Thomke, The Surprising Power of Online Experiments (Harvard Business Review, 2017)
The Bing ad-headline story: a shelved idea that raised revenue 12% (over $100M a year in the US) once tested; argues for experimentation over intuition.
Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu, Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications (CHI 2010)
Google's HEART framework and the Goals, Signals, Metrics process; the clearest short paper on turning product goals into metrics.
Zinkevich, Rules of Machine Learning (Google for Developers)
Rule 1 (launch without ML first), Rule 2 (design metrics first) and Rule 39 (launch decisions are a proxy for long-term goals) are product judgement for ML engineers.
Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Cambridge University Press, 2020)
The standard book on experiment-driven product decisions; its website lists chapters and resources.
Dmitriev, Gupta, Kim & Vaz, A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls in Online Controlled Experiments (KDD 2017)
Real Microsoft experiments where the metric moved for the wrong reason; useful background for every later topic in this track.

t: From product goal to metrics: north-star, driver and input metrics, guardrails and counter-metrics, what makes a good metric, and ratio-metric traps
sum: How to turn a product goal into a metric set: goals, signals and metrics (HEART), the north-star metric and the driver tree beneath it, guardrails and counter-metrics, the properties of a good metric with a sensitivity calculation, and the ratio-metric traps that fool experienced teams.
prereq: ps1
Product sense starts from users and a one-sentence goal; metrics come before the solution, and each metric should drive a decision.
math7
An A/B test's minimum detectable effect depends on the metric's variance and the sample size; ratio metrics whose denominator is not the randomisation unit need the delta method for their variance.
ml16
Offline model metrics and online business metrics can disagree; online metrics decide launches.
why:
A team running a news app decides that success means more page views. It is easy to measure, it rises when people read more, and the advertising team likes it. Over the next quarter they ship a redesign that buries the search box and splits long articles across several pages. Page views per user rise 18%. The team celebrates. Two months later, weekly returning users are down 6%, and user research finds people describing the app as "a maze". The redesign raised page views by making people work harder to get what they came for, and the metric rewarded it.

Nothing in this story required bad intentions. The team picked a metric that moves when users get value and when they are frustrated, then optimised it. Google's HEART paper uses almost exactly this example: a rise in page views for a feature "may occur because the feature is genuinely popular, or because a confusing interface leads users to get lost in it, clicking around to figure out how to escape." Microsoft's experimentation team found a bug in Bing that degraded search results and made queries per user rise over 10% and revenue per user over 30%; by the metrics on the dashboard, a broken search engine looked like a triumph.

Choosing metrics is where product goals become numbers that teams, models and launch reviews optimise. Get it wrong and every later step, from the model's training label to the experiment's verdict, inherits the error. Get it right and a team can make hundreds of decisions a year without arguing about what success means.

This lesson covers how to go from a goal to signals to metrics; the north-star metric and the tree of driver metrics beneath it, with a worked decomposition; guardrails and counter-metrics; the properties that make a metric good for decisions, including a sensitivity calculation showing why revenue makes a poor experiment metric; and the ratio-metric traps that catch experienced teams. The real cases are the HEART paper, Bing's puzzling outcome and two MSN experiments from Microsoft's "dirty dozen" of metric pitfalls.
primer:
A metric is a number computed from logged events or survey answers, defined precisely enough that two analysts would get the same value: what is counted (the numerator), over what (the denominator), in what time window, from which data source. A metric set is the handful of metrics a team uses to decide whether a change was good. Choosing a metric set is the step that turns "help users cook more" into something a dashboard, an experiment and a model can work with.

An analogy: running a restaurant. The owner's real goal is a restaurant people love and come back to. The best single measure of that is perhaps repeat visits per customer per month: it rises when food, service and value are good, and the owner cannot fake it easily. That is the north-star metric. Underneath it sit things the staff can influence directly: how long guests wait for a table, how long food takes, how often a dish is sent back, what share of first-time guests get a welcome. These are driver metrics (also called input metrics): each team can move its own, and together they produce the north star. Then there are things that must not get worse while chasing the north star: food-safety inspections, staff overtime, the cost of ingredients per plate. These are guardrails. Finally, if the kitchen is rewarded for speed, someone should watch dishes sent back, because the easiest way to cook faster is to cook worse. That is a counter-metric: chosen specifically to catch the most likely way a target could be gamed.

Where the analogy breaks: a restaurant owner can taste the food and watch the dining room. A product team with millions of users sees almost nothing directly; everything it knows comes through logged events and occasional surveys. That makes the choice of what to log, and how to turn it into metrics, far more consequential than it is for the restaurant. It also means the metrics can be corrupted in ways no diner would allow: bots, logging bugs, double-counted events, changes in what counts as a "session".

Three ideas carry most of the weight in this lesson. First, metrics come from goals through observable signals, not from whatever is easy to log. Second, a metric set has roles: one metric decides, a few protect, and the rest explain. Third, many metrics are ratios, and ratios can move because their denominator changed rather than because users behaved differently, which is the single most common way experienced teams misread results.

A fourth, quieter idea runs underneath: a metric is a tool for making decisions, and its quality depends on the decision it serves. A metric that is perfect for a quarterly business review (company-wide monthly users) can be useless for deciding whether a two-week experiment worked, because the experiment cannot move it detectably. A metric that is perfect for an experiment (clicks on a module per user) can be misleading on a dashboard if nobody remembers what it leaves out. The same team needs different metrics for different decisions, and naming which decision a metric serves is half of choosing it well.

Here is what the three roles sound like in a single sentence, which is roughly how you would say it in an interview: "We'll ship the new checkout if completed orders per active customer rise by at least 2% (the primary metric), as long as payment errors and page latency do not get significantly worse (guardrails) and refunds per order do not rise (the counter-metric for 'we made people buy things they did not want'); funnel steps will tell us where any change came from (diagnostics)." Notice that every metric has a role, a direction and a reason to be there. That sentence is the target output of this lesson.
body:
1. From goal to signals to metrics

Google's HEART paper (Rodden, Hutchinson and Fu, CHI 2010) describes a three-step process that remains the clearest way to go from a goal to metrics. First, state the goal: what are users trying to accomplish, and what is this change trying to achieve? Second, list the signals: observable behaviours or attitudes that would indicate success or failure. Third, define metrics from those signals, precisely enough to put on a dashboard and test in an experiment.

The paper's tips are worth repeating because they are where teams go wrong. At the goal step, team members often disagree about what the goal is, and the process is a chance to reach agreement; and do not worry yet about whether you can measure it. At the signal step, choose signals that are "sensitive and specific to the goal": they should move only when the experience gets better or worse, not for unrelated reasons. Also, failure is sometimes easier to see than success: abandoning a task, pressing undo, rage-clicking. At the metric step, normalise raw counts (they rise with the user base) into ratios, percentages or per-user averages, and filter out traffic from automated sources.

Worked example: a calendar app adds "smart scheduling", which proposes meeting times. Goal: "help people schedule meetings with less back-and-forth". Signals of success: users accept a proposed time; the meeting is not rescheduled; the scheduling thread ends sooner. Signals of failure: users dismiss the proposals and pick manually; meetings proposed by the feature get moved within a day. Metrics: share of new meetings created from a proposal (adoption of the feature), median number of messages between the first request and a confirmed meeting (task success, the primary), and the share of feature-scheduled meetings rescheduled within 24 hours (a failure signal that works as a counter-metric). Notice that "number of proposals shown" never appears: it measures the feature's activity, not its value.

2. HEART and PULSE: a checklist of metric categories

The HEART paper contrasts two families. PULSE metrics are the business and technical health metrics most companies already track: Page views, Uptime, Latency, Seven-day active users and Earnings. They matter, but they are indirect measures of user experience and can be ambiguous; the paper notes that seven-day active users could in theory rise even with 100% weekly turnover of the user base.

HEART is a set of user-centred categories to choose from: Happiness (attitudes: satisfaction, perceived ease, likelihood to recommend, usually from surveys), Engagement (frequency, intensity or depth of use, reported per user), Adoption (new users of a product or feature in a period), Retention (users from one period still active in a later one) and Task success (efficiency, effectiveness, error rate). The paper's examples are concrete: Gmail measured engagement as the percentage of active users who visited on five or more days in the last week, and found it strongly predictive of longer-term retention; iGoogle saw satisfaction drop after a redesign and then recover, which suggested change aversion rather than a worse design; Google Finance used adoption and retention to separate crisis-driven new visitors from existing users checking their portfolios during the September 2008 market crash.

The useful habit is not to measure all five but to run through them deliberately and decide which apply. An enterprise tool used as part of someone's job may not need engagement at all (people use it because they must), but task success matters a lot. A new feature needs adoption; a mature product cares more about retention.

3. The north-star metric

A north-star metric is the single number a product organisation treats as the best measurable summary of the value it delivers to users. It exists to align many teams: if search, recommendations, notifications and onboarding all agree that, say, "weekly completed orders per active customer" is what matters, their local decisions point in the same direction.

Good north stars share five properties. They reflect value received by users (an order delivered, a meeting scheduled, a song listened to and saved) rather than effort spent (searches, clicks, page views), because effort can rise when the product gets worse. They are normalised or tied to a unit of value, so they do not rise merely because more users signed up. They lead revenue: when the north star rises, revenue tends to follow later, but the north star responds sooner and is less noisy. They are understandable by everyone in the company. And they decompose into drivers that individual teams can move.

Bad north stars usually fail on the first property. Time spent rewards both delight and confusion; queries per user rewards both curiosity and failed searches; messages sent rewards both conversation and spam. When an interviewer gives you an effort metric as the goal, the senior move is to propose a value-based version and to keep the effort metric as a diagnostic.

In product-type terms (hypothetical examples, since companies rarely publish their exact definitions): a marketplace's north star is often completed transactions per active buyer; a collaboration tool's is often weekly active teams performing the core action (editing a shared document, sending a message in a channel); a media product's is often engaged consumption (listening or watching time weighted by some satisfaction signal); a subscription utility's is often successful task completions per subscriber.

4. Driver metrics and metric trees, with a worked decomposition

A north star is too high-level for most teams to move directly, and when it changes you need to know why. A metric tree decomposes it into the factors that produce it. The most useful decompositions are multiplicative, because each factor is something a different team owns.

Worked example. Dishly is a hypothetical food-delivery app. Weekly orders can be written as:

orders = weekly active users × sessions per user × orders per session

Last week: 2,000,000 weekly active users × 3.0 sessions per user × 0.12 orders per session = 720,000 orders. This week orders fell to about 684,000, a 5% drop. The factors moved as follows: users 2,000,000 → 1,980,000 (−1%), sessions per user 3.0 → 3.03 (+1%), orders per session 0.12 → 0.114 (−5%). Check: 1,980,000 × 3.03 × 0.114 ≈ 683,950.

Because the log of a product is the sum of the logs, each factor's share of the change is its log change divided by the total log change. Here: ln(0.99) = −0.0101, ln(1.01) = +0.0100, ln(0.95) = −0.0513, total −0.0514. Users explain about 20% of the drop, sessions per user offset about 19%, and orders per session explain essentially all of it. The investigation should start at checkout and restaurant availability, not acquisition. This is the same move ps4 uses to diagnose metric changes; here it shows why trees are worth building in advance.

Trees can also be additive by segment: orders = orders from new users + orders from returning users, or the sum over cities. Additive decompositions answer "where" a change happened; multiplicative ones answer "which step". In practice you use both: first find the segment, then the step.

Driver metrics are what individual teams adopt as their targets. The onboarding team owns new-user activation, the search team owns orders per session, the notifications team owns sessions per user. The danger, which the next section addresses, is that each team then optimises its driver at the others' expense.

5. Guardrails and counter-metrics

A guardrail metric is one that is not the goal but must not get significantly worse. Microsoft's experimentation team describes guardrails as metrics "not clearly indicative of success of the feature being tested", which "we do not want to significantly harm when making a ship decision", with page load time as the classic example: almost any feature slightly increases it, so the question is how much is acceptable. Guardrails fall into four families:

  • User experience: latency, crash rate, error rate, accessibility regressions.
  • Business: revenue, cost per user, support tickets per thousand users.
  • Ecosystem: the other side of a marketplace or network (seller revenue, creator uploads, driver earnings).
  • Trust and safety: reports, blocks, policy-violation prevalence, unsubscribes.

A counter-metric is narrower. It is chosen for a particular primary metric to catch the most likely way that metric could be improved without delivering value. Examples:

Primary metricEasy way to game itCounter-metric
Notification opens per userSend more notificationsNotifications disabled per thousand users
Video starts per userClickbait thumbnailsStarts abandoned in under 10 seconds
Support tickets closed per agent-hourClose tickets prematurelyTickets reopened within 7 days
Suggestions accepted per userShow more, safer suggestionsAccepted suggestions later deleted
Conversion rateSteep discountsMargin per order, refund rate

For every guardrail, decide in advance what change would block a launch. "Must not get worse" is not a rule a launch review can apply; "p95 latency must not rise by more than 20 milliseconds, and crash rate must not rise by a statistically significant amount" is. ps7 covers how to handle borderline guardrail movements.

6. What makes a good decision metric

Six properties matter for a metric that will decide launches. A metric need not be perfect on all six; the point is to know where each candidate is weak.

Sensitive: a real effect of plausible size produces a statistically detectable change within the experiment's duration. Attributable: when it moves, the movement comes from the change being tested, not from seasonality, marketing campaigns or other teams' launches (randomised experiments help a lot here, because both arms see the same outside world). Hard to game: it is difficult to raise without delivering the value it stands for. Cheap and fast to compute: available daily from existing logs, not requiring a quarterly survey. Directional: everyone agrees which direction is good (time spent fails this). Normalised: per user or per unit, so arms of different sizes and periods of growth are comparable. Google's Rules of Machine Learning compresses several of these into Rule 13: "choose a simple, observable and attributable metric for your first objective".

Sensitivity is the property most often ignored, and it can be calculated. From math7, an experiment with n users per arm can detect, with 80% power at 5% significance, an absolute difference of about (1.96 + 0.84) × sqrt(2σ²/n) = 2.8 × sqrt(2σ²/n), where σ is the metric's standard deviation across users. Dividing by the mean gives the minimum detectable effect (MDE) in relative terms. Compare three candidate metrics for a shopping app with n = 50,000 per arm:

MetricMeanStd devAbsolute MDERelative MDE
Weekly return rate (yes/no)0.400.490.00872.2%
Sessions per user3.24.00.0712.2%
Revenue per user$2.00$15.00$0.2713.3%
Revenue per user, capped at $50$1.80$6.00$0.115.9%

The arithmetic for revenue: 2.8 × sqrt(2 × 225 / 50,000) = 2.8 × 0.0949 = 0.266, which is 13.3% of $2.00. Revenue per user is heavy-tailed: a few large spenders produce a standard deviation many times the mean. Most product changes move revenue by a percent or two, so an experiment using raw revenue as its primary metric will come back "no significant change" almost every time. Winsorising, capping values at a high percentile, cuts the variance sharply (the capped row assumes a cap at $50 changes the mean slightly and the standard deviation a lot). Other options are using a conversion rate as the primary and revenue as a guardrail, or variance-reduction techniques such as CUPED (math7). The general lesson: before choosing a primary metric, estimate its MDE at the sample size you can afford.

7. Ratio-metric traps

Many important metrics are ratios: click-through rate (CTR, clicks over impressions), conversion rate, revenue per session, average page load time. A ratio can change because its numerator changed, because its denominator changed, or because the population it is computed over changed. Four traps follow.

Trap 1: the denominator moved. In an experiment described in Microsoft's "dirty dozen" paper (Dmitriev et al., KDD 2017), a module near the bottom of the home page of MSN (Microsoft's news and web portal) was moved higher, so users had to scroll less to reach it. The module's CTR fell by 40%. Checked separately, both parts rose: clicks on the module by 74%, the number of times it was displayed by 200%. A ratio of 1.74 / 3.00 = 0.58 is a 42% drop, matching the headline. Moving the module up showed it to many people who were less interested, so the share who clicked fell while the total benefit grew; whole-page CTR stayed flat and revenue rose. The experiment was a success that its main metric called a failure.

Trap 2: the population changed (metric sample ratio mismatch). In another MSN experiment, links opened in a new tab instead of the same tab. Average home-page load time rose 8.32%. The cause: the treatment had 7.8% fewer home-page loads, because users no longer pressed the back button to return (the home page was still open in the old tab), and back-button reloads are fast thanks to browser caching. Removing many fast loads from the average made the remaining average slower, without any page actually loading more slowly. When the denominator's population differs between arms, the ratio compares different things.

Trap 3: average of ratios versus ratio of totals. Take two users. User A saw 100 impressions and clicked 10 (10%). User B saw 2 and clicked 1 (50%). The ratio of totals is 11 / 102 = 10.8%; the average of ratios (per-user CTR, averaged) is (10% + 50%) / 2 = 30%. The first is dominated by heavy users; the second treats every user equally. If a change improves the experience of light users and slightly worsens heavy users, the two definitions can move in opposite directions. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Pick one deliberately, write it down, and keep it fixed across experiments.

Trap 4: wrong variance. When users are randomised but the metric's denominator is impressions or sessions (ratio of totals), the impressions are not independent: one user's sessions are correlated. Treating each impression as an independent observation underestimates the variance and produces false positives. The delta method or a bootstrap that resamples users (math7) gives correct intervals.

The practical rule for all four: for every ratio metric in a decision, also look at its numerator and denominator as per-user metrics, and check whether the denominator's population changed between arms.

8. Putting it together: a metric set

Before assembling the set, two choices remain that beginners often skip: the time window and the unit.

Time window. The same behaviour can be measured per day, per week or per experiment period, and the choice changes what the metric rewards. Daily metrics are noisy for products people use a few times a week: a recipe app's "cooked today" is mostly zeros. Weekly windows smooth out day-of-week patterns (many products have weekend peaks), so a change that shifts usage from Saturday to Sunday does not look like a win or a loss. For experiments, a common pattern is "per user over the whole experiment period": each user contributes one number, such as total orders during the three weeks, which keeps the unit of analysis equal to the unit of randomisation and simplifies the variance calculation.

Unit. Per user, per session, per page view and per request answer different questions. Per-session metrics can be gamed by changing what counts as a session (shorter timeouts create more, shorter sessions). Per-user metrics are the default for decisions because users are what experiments randomise and what businesses retain. When a metric is naturally per session (orders per session), compute it, but also report its per-user counterpart (orders per user), because a change that splits one long session into two short ones can raise sessions per user and lower orders per session while nothing real changed.

A worked check of why the unit matters: suppose a treatment shortens the session timeout from 30 to 15 minutes. Before, a typical user has 3.0 sessions a week and 0.36 orders, so 0.12 orders per session. After, the same behaviour is split into 3.6 sessions, so orders per session read 0.10, a 17% "drop", and sessions per user a 20% "rise". Orders per user, unchanged at 0.36, shows correctly that nothing happened.

Back to the calendar app's smart scheduling. A complete metric set reads: primary, median messages from first request to confirmed meeting, per scheduling thread (lower is better, task success); counter-metric, share of feature-scheduled meetings rescheduled within 24 hours; guardrails, calendar-page latency at the 95th percentile, weekly active users' next-week return rate, and support tickets about scheduling; diagnostics, proposal acceptance rate and the share of threads where proposals were shown. Each has a role, a direction and, for the guardrails, a blocking threshold. Note what this set does not contain: proposals shown (activity, not value) and total meetings created (rises with growth).
deep:
Composite metrics and the OEC

Microsoft's experimentation literature uses the term OEC (Overall Evaluation Criterion) for the metric that decides an experiment. Ideally it is a single metric; when the goal has parts that trade off, it can be a weighted combination, such as revenue per user minus a penalty proportional to ad load. A composite makes the trade-off explicit, so different teams' launches are judged consistently instead of being argued case by case. Its costs are that the weights encode a value judgement that someone must own and revisit, and that a composite can hide which component moved. The usual practice is to decide on the composite but always report its components next to it.

Validating a proxy across experiments, not across users

Most decision metrics are proxies for something slower: next-quarter retention, lifetime value. The tempting validation is to show that users with a high proxy also have high retention. That correlation is almost guaranteed and almost useless, because engaged users score high on everything. The test that matters is whether interventions that move the proxy also move the long-term outcome.
