With a history of past experiments, plot each experiment's effect on the proxy against its effect on the long-term outcome; a proxy is good if the points line up with a positive slope. Duolingo's former product lead describes a related approach: modelling how changes in each retention rate would compound into daily active users before choosing which one to target (ps5).

Leading and lagging indicators

A lagging indicator, such as 90-day retention, is close to what the business cares about but only measurable after a long delay. A leading indicator, such as the Gmail-style "visited on five or more of the last seven days", responds within days and predicts the lagging one. Experiments need leading indicators; strategy reviews need lagging ones. The work is in connecting them: an organisation that tracks only leading indicators drifts towards whatever is easy to move this week, and one that tracks only lagging indicators cannot run experiments at all.

Metric definitions are code, and they drift

"Weekly active user" sounds unambiguous until you ask: active doing what (opening the app, or doing the core action)? Counted by user account or by device? In which time zone does the week start? Are logged-out users included? Large companies keep a metric catalogue in which each metric's definition is versioned code with an owner, because two dashboards disagreeing by 3% can consume weeks of meetings. When a logging change alters a definition, mature teams back-fill or annotate the series so that the change is not mistaken for user behaviour. Interviewers like candidates who ask "how is that metric defined?" before reasoning about it.

Sensitivity as a design goal

Because the MDE scales with σ / mean and with 1 / sqrt(n), there are only three ways to detect smaller effects: more users, longer experiments, or lower-variance metrics. The third is often the cheapest. Options include capping outliers, using binary versions of continuous metrics ("did the user order at least once?" instead of "how many orders?"), measuring only users who were actually exposed to the change (triggered analysis, which removes users whose experience could not have changed and therefore dilute the effect), and adjusting for pre-experiment behaviour (CUPED, in math7). Microsoft and others report that teams spend real effort building metrics designed for sensitivity, because a metric that never reaches significance cannot guide decisions.

Effort metrics versus success metrics

A recurring pattern from Bing's puzzling outcomes: when users fail, they work harder, and many engagement metrics measure work. Queries per user rise when results are bad; time in a settings page rises when it is confusing; messages to support rise when a product breaks. The defence is to pair every effort metric with a success metric: queries per session with time to a successful click; support messages with resolution rate. When an effort metric jumps and the paired success metric does not, assume something got worse.

Where Goodhart's law starts

Once a metric becomes a target that teams or models optimise, it starts to lose its connection to the thing it measured, because optimisation finds the cheapest ways to move the number. A fuller treatment, including what happens when a model rather than a team does the optimising, is in ps3; here it is enough to say that counter-metrics, periodic re-validation of proxies, and rotating the specific driver targets are the practical defences.

Metrics for two-sided products

In a marketplace or a network, each side has its own north star, and the platform's real goal is a healthy exchange between them. A ride-hailing app's riders care about pick-up time and price; its drivers care about earnings per hour. A metric set that measures only riders will approve changes that quietly lower driver earnings, which shows up months later as fewer drivers, longer pick-up times and worse rider metrics. The standard practice is a primary metric on the side the change targets, plus at least one guardrail on the other side, plus a marketplace-health metric such as the share of requests fulfilled. Experiments on one side also leak to the other (riders in the treatment compete for the same drivers as riders in control), which is why ps6 treats marketplace experiments separately.

Survey-based metrics

HEART's Happiness category relies on attitudes, which logs cannot see: satisfaction, perceived ease, regret. Survey metrics catch failures that behaviour hides, such as people who keep using a product they dislike because switching is costly. Their weaknesses are low response rates, response bias (unhappy or very happy users answer more), and small samples per experiment arm. Practical patterns are a short in-product survey shown to a random sample (one question, a five-point scale), tracked as a weekly series rather than as an experiment metric; and, at larger scale, training a model to predict survey answers for everyone from behaviour, then validating it on held-back responses. YouTube describes doing exactly that for "valued watchtime" (ps3). The model's prediction then becomes a metric, with all the proxy caveats that implies.
prod:
The real case: Bing's puzzling outcome

In "Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: Five Puzzling Outcomes Explained" (Kohavi, Deng, Frasca, Longbotham, Walker and Xu, KDD 2012), the first puzzle comes from Bing. A bug in an experiment's treatment showed users very poor search results. Two of the organisation's key metrics improved dramatically: distinct queries per user went up over 10% and revenue per user over 30%. The paper asks how Bing should evaluate experiments if a broken product can look like a big win, and answers that the long-term goals (query share and revenue) "do not align with short-term measurements in experiments. If they did, we would intentionally degrade quality to raise query share and revenue!"

The explanation is that degraded results force people to issue more queries and click more on ads, which the authors compare to raising prices in a shop: short-term revenue rises, but customers move to the competition over time. Their fix was a decomposition. Monthly distinct queries equal users per month × sessions per user × distinct queries per session. In a randomised experiment, users per arm are fixed by the design, so that term cannot be the target. Distinct queries per session should fall when search works well, because users find answers with fewer queries. The term that captures users choosing to come back is sessions per user, and that is what the paper recommends optimising. The later "dirty dozen" paper from the same group refers to sessions per user as "the key Bing metric".

The production lessons: a north star that rewards user effort can be raised by making the product worse; decomposing the top-level goal reveals which component reflects value; and when a change produces a dramatic win, check whether users are winning or merely working harder.

Failure modes you will see

Metric definition changes masquerading as behaviour. A logging library upgrade starts counting app foregrounds as sessions; sessions per user jump 7% overnight. Symptom: a step change on a single day across all segments, coinciding with a release. Defence: annotate deployments on metric charts and keep a data-quality metric (events per user per client version) that spots instrumentation changes.

Bots and internal traffic. Automated traffic inflates counts and dilutes ratios. A crawler that loads pages without clicking lowers CTR. The HEART paper lists filtering automated traffic as one of the challenges of log-based metrics. Defence: standard bot filters before metrics are computed, and monitoring of the share of traffic filtered.

Teams gaming drivers. When a team's bonus or roadmap depends on a driver metric, its members will find ways to move it, some of which do not help users. Symptom: the driver rises steadily while the north star is flat. Defence: counter-metrics owned by someone else, and reviewing driver metrics against the north star each quarter.

Too many metrics, no decision rule. An experiment scorecard with 200 metrics shows ten significant changes, some up, some down, and the launch meeting debates which matter. Defence: pre-declared primary and guardrails with thresholds; everything else is labelled diagnostic and cannot block or justify a launch on its own.

Tools and practice

Companies that run many experiments typically have a metric layer (a catalogue of definitions computed the same way for dashboards and experiments), an experimentation platform that computes the standard scorecard for every test (in10 designs one), automated checks for sample ratio mismatch, and metric review meetings where new metrics are proposed with evidence of sensitivity and of alignment with long-term outcomes. For an ML engineer, the relevant practice is to insist that the online metric for a model launch comes from that shared layer rather than a bespoke notebook, so results are comparable across launches.

How a metric review works

Mature experimentation organisations treat a new decision metric like a new API: someone proposes it with a written definition, evidence that it is sensitive (its MDE at typical experiment sizes), evidence that it is aligned (past experiments where it moved together with long-term outcomes), and a list of known ways it can be gamed. Reviewers check that it does not duplicate an existing metric under a new name, that its data source is reliable, and that it has an owner who will maintain it. Only then does it enter the standard scorecard. The process sounds bureaucratic, but it is cheaper than the alternative: two teams arguing about whose version of "active user" is right in the middle of a launch review.
myths: The north-star metric should be the company's revenue.

Revenue is an outcome of delivering value, and it lags, it is noisy, and it can be raised in the short term by harming users (more ads, higher prices). A north-star metric is chosen to capture the value users get, in a form that predicts revenue over time, such as completed orders per active customer or weekly active teams doing the core task. Revenue stays on the dashboard and usually as a guardrail or a business metric alongside it.
A higher click-through rate always means more relevant content.

Click-through rate is a ratio, and it falls whenever the denominator grows faster than the numerator. In a Microsoft experiment, moving an MSN module higher on the page cut its click-through rate by 40% while its clicks rose 74%, because impressions rose 200%; the change was good. Always read the numerator and denominator of a ratio separately before interpreting it.
More metrics in an experiment scorecard means a safer decision.

Every extra metric is another chance of a false positive: with 40 independent metrics at a 5% significance level, about two will look significant by chance. Teams that add metrics without designating which one decides end up cherry-picking. A small, pre-declared set (one primary, a few guardrails) with many diagnostics clearly labelled as such is safer.
A good metric is one that correlates with long-term success across users.

Correlation across users is easy to find and misleading: people who use a feature more are often already more engaged, so the feature looks predictive of retention even if it causes nothing. A useful proxy must move together with the long-term outcome across experiments (when you change it, the outcome changes), which is a much stricter test.
Guardrails are optional extras you add if you have time.

Guardrails are how you prevent a win on the primary metric from being bought with damage elsewhere: slower pages, more crashes, more complaints, fewer sellers. Most painful launches in experimentation write-ups improved the primary metric and quietly broke something nobody was watching. A metric set without guardrails is incomplete.

Goal: decompose a change in a top-level metric into its drivers and see which factor explains it, then see a ratio metric move the "wrong" way. About 15 minutes; Python 3.12 standard library only.

  1. Save as tree.py and run python tree.py:
import math

before = {"users": 2_000_000, "sessions_per_user": 3.00, "orders_per_session": 0.120}
after  = {"users": 1_980_000, "sessions_per_user": 3.03, "orders_per_session": 0.114}

def total(d):
    return math.prod(d.values())

t0, t1 = total(before), total(after)
print(f"orders {t0:,.0f} -> {t1:,.0f} ({t1 / t0 - 1:+.1%})")
log_total = math.log(t1 / t0)
for k in before:
    lc = math.log(after[k] / before[k])
    print(f"{k:20} {after[k] / before[k] - 1:+.1%}  share of change {lc / log_total:6.1%}")

# A ratio metric whose denominator moves: module moved up the page
clicks_c, imps_c = 1_000, 10_000
clicks_t, imps_t = round(clicks_c * 1.74), round(imps_c * 3.00)
print(f"CTR control {clicks_c / imps_c:.2%}, treatment {clicks_t / imps_t:.2%}")

What to look for: orders fall about 5%, and the "share of change" column shows orders per session explaining about 100% of the drop, users about 20%, and sessions per user about −19% (it pushed the other way). Shares sum to 100% because logs add. In the second part, CTR falls from 10% to 5.8% even though clicks rise 74%. Now experiment: change users in after to 1,900,000 and see the shares redistribute; then set treatment impressions to 1.5× and see CTR rise while the module is shown to fewer new people. Write one sentence explaining when you would report clicks per user instead of CTR.
recap: Turn goals into metrics in three steps (Google's HEART paper calls them goals, signals, metrics): state the goal, find user behaviours or attitudes that would show it is met, then define precise metrics from those signals.

A north-star metric is the single measurable summary of the value a product delivers; good ones are per user or per unit of value, lead revenue rather than equal it, and can be broken down into drivers.

A metric tree decomposes the north star into driver metrics, usually multiplicatively (users × sessions per user × conversion per session), so a change in the top can be attributed to the factor that moved.
Guardrail metrics must not get significantly worse (latency, crashes, complaints, the other side of a marketplace); counter-metrics catch the most likely way the primary metric could be gamed.
A good decision metric is sensitive (moves detectably within the experiment), attributable (moves because of the change), hard to game, cheap to compute, clearly directional and normalised.

Sensitivity can be computed: the minimum detectable relative effect is roughly 2.8 × sqrt(2σ²/n) divided by the mean, so heavy-tailed metrics such as revenue per user need far more users than retention or sessions per user.

Ratio metrics can move because the denominator changed rather than the behaviour you care about; always check numerator and denominator separately, as in Microsoft's MSN module that lost 40% CTR while gaining 74% more clicks.
The average of per-user ratios and the ratio of totals answer different questions and can differ hugely; pick one deliberately and keep it fixed.

Bing's bug that raised queries per user 10% and revenue per user 30% by degrading results shows why a north star must not reward users working harder; Bing's decomposition pointed to sessions per user instead.
glossary: Attributable
A property of a metric: when it moves in an experiment, the movement can be traced to the change being tested rather than to outside events or other teams' changes.
Average of ratios
A ratio metric computed per user and then averaged across users, giving each user equal weight regardless of activity.
Counter-metric
A metric paired with a primary metric to catch the most likely way the primary could be gamed or improved at someone's expense.
CTR
Click-through rate: clicks divided by impressions (times an item was shown).
CUPED

Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data: a variance-reduction method that adjusts each user's metric by their own pre-experiment value, often cutting the needed sample size substantially (math7).
Delta method
A statistical approximation for the variance of a ratio of two averages, needed when the ratio's denominator is not the unit that was randomised (math7).
Diagnostic metric
A metric used to explain why a primary metric moved, such as a funnel step, not used to decide launches.
Driver metric
A metric one level below the north star in a metric tree, which teams can influence directly and which combines with others to produce the north star; also called an input metric.
Goals, signals, metrics
A three-step process from Google's HEART paper: state the goal, identify behaviours or attitudes that indicate success, then define precise metrics from those signals.
Guardrail metric
A metric that is not the goal but must not get significantly worse; a significant guardrail regression can block a launch.
HEART
Google's user-experience metric categories: Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention and Task success.
Lagging indicator
A metric that reflects outcomes only after a delay, such as annual revenue or 90-day retention; hard to use for decisions within a short experiment.
Leading indicator
A metric that moves early and predicts a later outcome, such as first-week activity predicting 90-day retention.
MDE
Minimum detectable effect: the smallest true change an experiment of a given size has a good chance (usually 80%) of detecting.
Metric sample ratio mismatch
A situation where the set of events a metric is computed over differs between treatment and control (for example, fewer page loads), so the metric compares different populations.
Metric tree
A decomposition of a top-level metric into the factors that produce it, often multiplicative, used to attribute changes and to give teams metrics they can move.
North-star metric
The one metric a product organisation treats as the best measurable summary of the value it delivers to users.
OEC
Overall Evaluation Criterion: the metric or weighted combination that decides an experiment's success.
PULSE
The HEART paper's name for common business and technical metrics: Page views, Uptime, Latency, Seven-day active users and Earnings.
Ratio of totals
A ratio metric computed by summing the numerator and denominator over all users first, so heavy users dominate.
Sensitivity
How readily a metric shows a statistically significant change when a real effect exists; depends on its variance relative to its mean and on the sample size.
Signal
In the HEART process, an observable user behaviour or attitude that would indicate a goal is being met, such as returning daily or rating a session highly.
Triggered analysis
Analysing only the users whose experience could actually differ between arms (for example, those who opened the changed screen), which removes dilution and increases sensitivity.
Winsorising
Capping extreme values of a metric at a chosen percentile to reduce variance and the influence of outliers.
drill:
Metric design drill

Trailhead is a hypothetical hiking app (3 million monthly users) launching offline maps for subscribers. The product manager (PM) proposes "map downloads per week" as the success metric. Propose a better metric set with roles, and estimate whether your primary metric can detect a 3% effect with 40,000 subscribers per arm.

Answer

Why downloads is weak: it measures activity, not value (people download maps they never use), it rises if the download button is made more prominent, and it is not normalised.

Goal: help subscribers navigate confidently where there is no signal, so they hike more with the app and stay subscribed.

Primary: recorded hikes per weekly active subscriber (a hike with GPS tracking for at least 1 km). Counter-metric: downloaded maps never opened within 30 days. Guardrails: subscription cancellations, app storage-related uninstalls, crash rate on map screens, support tickets about storage. Diagnostics: share of hikes that used an offline map; hikes in areas with poor signal.

Sensitivity: assume a mean of 0.9 recorded hikes per weekly subscriber with standard deviation 1.4. Absolute MDE ≈ 2.8 × sqrt(2 × 1.96 / 40,000) = 2.8 × sqrt(0.000098) = 2.8 × 0.0099 = 0.0277, which is 3.1% of 0.9. So 40,000 per arm is just about enough for a 3% effect over one week of data; running three or four weeks and using hikes over the whole period per subscriber lowers relative variance further, and limiting the analysis to subscribers who open the map screen (triggered analysis) helps more. If the expected effect were 1%, the answer would be "this metric cannot detect it at this size; use the share of hikes in low-signal areas, where the effect should be concentrated".
qa: E
What is a north-star metric, and what makes a good one?

It is the single metric that best summarises the value a product delivers to its users, used to align many teams' decisions. A good one reflects value to users rather than effort or exposure, is normalised (per user or per unit) so it does not rise just because the user base grew, leads long-term revenue, and can be decomposed into drivers that teams can move. Weekly completed orders per active customer is a reasonable example for a delivery app; page views is a poor one.
E
What is the difference between a guardrail and a counter-metric?

A guardrail is any metric that must not get significantly worse, whatever the change: latency, crash rate, unsubscribes, revenue. A counter-metric is chosen specifically for a given primary metric to catch the most likely way it could be gamed, such as 'notifications disabled' alongside 'notification opens'. Every counter-metric acts as a guardrail, but not every guardrail is a counter-metric.
E
Why prefer per-user metrics over totals?

Totals rise when more users arrive, so they confuse growth with improvement and are not comparable between experiment arms of different sizes. Per-user averages or rates ask whether each user's experience got better. Google's HEART paper makes this recommendation explicitly for engagement metrics.
M
Walk me through goals, signals and metrics for a photo-sharing app's new editing tools.

Goal: help users make photos they are proud to share. Signals: users who open the editor go on to post the edited photo; they use the tools again; they rate edits highly in a sample survey; failure shows up as abandoning the editor or undoing all changes. Metrics: share-after-edit rate per editor session (primary), weekly editor users who return the next week, and 'revert all' rate as a failure signal, with app latency and crash rate as guardrails.

Follow-up: Why not use time spent in the editor? — Time in the editor rises when the tools are confusing as much as when they are delightful, so its direction is ambiguous; the HEART paper gives the same warning about page views.
M
Build a metric tree for weekly orders at a food-delivery app and explain how you would use it.

Weekly orders = weekly active users × sessions per user × orders per session. If orders fall 5%, compute the change in each factor; for example users −1%, sessions per user +1% and conversion −5% means conversion explains nearly all of it, so I would look at the checkout funnel, prices and restaurant availability rather than acquisition. The log of a product is the sum of the logs, so each factor's share of the change is its log change over the total log change.
M
A module moved higher on a page and its click-through rate fell 40%. Is that bad?

Not necessarily. CTR is clicks over impressions; moving the module up shows it to many more people, including less interested ones, so impressions can grow faster than clicks. In Microsoft's MSN example the module's clicks rose 74% and its impressions 200%, so CTR fell while the module was more useful, and revenue rose. I would read numerator and denominator separately and check whole-page clicks.
Follow-up: What metric would you use instead? — Clicks on the module per user and whole-page clicks or successful sessions per user, which keep the denominator fixed at the randomised unit.
M
Why is revenue per user often a poor primary metric for an experiment?

It is heavy-tailed: a few large spenders create a standard deviation many times the mean, so the minimum detectable effect is large. With a mean of $2 and a standard deviation of $15, 50,000 users per arm can only detect about a 13% change. Capping (winsorising) extreme values, using a conversion rate, or using a leading indicator makes the experiment sensitive enough; revenue can still be a guardrail with a looser threshold.
M
What is the difference between an average of per-user ratios and a ratio of totals? When does it matter?

The average of ratios gives every user equal weight; the ratio of totals lets heavy users dominate. Two users, one with 10 clicks in 100 impressions and one with 1 in 2, have a ratio of totals of 10.8% but an average of ratios of 30%. If a change affects light and heavy users differently, the two versions can move in opposite directions, so choose one deliberately, state it, and keep it fixed across experiments.

Follow-up: Which needs special variance treatment? — The ratio of totals when users are randomised, because its unit of analysis (impressions) differs from the unit of randomisation (users); the delta method or bootstrapping by user handles it.
M
What makes a metric 'hard to game'?

It is hard to raise without delivering the value it stands for. Clicks are easy to game with sensational thumbnails; completed purchases that are not refunded are harder. Ways to harden a metric are to measure an outcome rather than an action, to pair it with a counter-metric, to exclude low-quality events (short visits, bot traffic), and to weight by satisfaction where you have a signal.
H
Bing once saw queries per user rise over 10% and revenue per user over 30% in an experiment. Why was that bad, and what metric did they recommend?

A bug degraded the search results, so users had to search more and clicked more ads; both numbers rose because the product got worse. Kohavi and colleagues decomposed monthly distinct queries into users × sessions per user × distinct queries per session, and argued that queries per session should fall when search works (users find answers faster), while sessions per user (users choosing to come back) is the component to increase. Sessions per user became the key metric.

Follow-up: How would you detect that kind of failure in your own product? — Pair effort metrics with success metrics, such as queries per session with time to a successful click, and treat any large win in an effort metric as suspicious.
H
How do you validate that a proxy metric predicts the long-term outcome you care about?

Correlation across users is not enough, because engaged users do everything more. The stronger test is across experiments: collect many past experiments, and check that the ones that moved the proxy also moved the long-term outcome in the same direction and in proportion. If you lack enough experiments, a few long-running holdouts can calibrate the relationship. Without that, call the proxy a hypothesis.
H
Design the metric set for a marketplace feature that recommends lower prices to sellers.

Primary: completed transactions per active buyer, since lower prices should help buyers find deals. Seller-side guardrails: seller revenue per active seller and seller churn, because the feature could transfer value from sellers to buyers and drive them away. Counter-metric: share of listings priced below a floor (race to the bottom). Diagnostics: price-change acceptance rate and time to sale. Because sellers compete for the same buyers, an experiment randomising sellers will overstate the effect; I would flag that interference (ps6).
H
When would you use a composite OEC instead of a single primary metric?

When the goal genuinely has several parts that trade off, such as revenue and user experience in ads, and the team can agree on the exchange rate between them. A composite such as revenue per user minus a penalty times an ad-load measure makes the trade-off explicit and decides launches consistently. The risks are that the weights are arbitrary and that a composite can hide which part moved, so I would always report the components alongside it.
