t: From product metric to ML objective: proxy labels and the gap, multi-objective scores, Goodhart's law, and choosing what the model optimises
sum: How a product goal becomes a training label and a ranking score: the labels you can observe and how far each sits from value, the proxy gap worked with numbers, multi-objective value models and how to set their weights, Goodhart's law in four forms, ecosystem objectives, and YouTube's move from clicks to watch time to valued watch time.
prereq: ps2
A north-star metric reflects value to users; guardrails and counter-metrics protect it; proxies must be validated across experiments, not across users.
ml7
Calibrated probabilities mean a predicted 0.2 happens about 20% of the time; ranking metrics such as AUC ignore calibration, but adding predicted probabilities together requires it.
rec6
Ranking models can have several output heads (click, like, share, watch time) trained together on shared features, then combined into one score.
rec10
Logged behaviour is shaped by what the system showed: position bias, selection bias and feedback loops make labels reflect the old policy, not just user preference.
why:
A short-video app trains its first ranking model to predict clicks. It works: click-through rate rises 9% in the experiment, and the model ships. Within a month the content team notices that the top of the feed is full of videos with shocking thumbnails and titles that the videos do not deliver on. Users click, watch four seconds, and leave. Click-through is at a record high and complaints are too.

The team switches the label to watch time. Now the feed fills with long compilations and endless clips that people half-watch late at night. Average watch time per user rises 12%. Survey scores fall, and a growing share of users say they "wasted time" on the app. The team has optimised two different labels, and each time the model faithfully delivered more of the label and less of what anyone wanted.

The engineers did nothing wrong technically. The models were well trained; offline metrics improved; the experiments were run properly. The failure was upstream, in the choice of what to optimise. A model is a powerful optimiser of whatever objective it is given, and the gap between the objective and the product goal is exactly where it will find its gains. This is the most consequential product decision an ML engineer makes, and it is often made in an afternoon by whoever writes the training pipeline.

This lesson is about closing that gap. It covers the labels you can actually observe and how far each sits from value; a worked example where three objectives pick three different winners; how production systems combine several predicted outcomes into one score, and how to set the weights; Goodhart's law in its four forms, with ranking examples; how to handle ecosystem goals like creator health; and YouTube's public account of moving from clicks to watch time to survey-based "valued watchtime", including the 20% drop in views it accepted along the way.

A note on scope: the examples are mostly feeds and search, because that is where the public evidence is richest, but the same chain applies to fraud models (what counts as fraud, and what does a false block cost?), ETA predictors (is the goal accuracy, or riders not being surprised?) and LLM assistants (is the goal a high rating, or the task actually done?). The last part of the body shows those translations.
primer:
Supervised models learn from labels: observed outcomes attached to past examples. A ranking model for a feed is trained on past impressions (times an item was shown) labelled with what happened: was it clicked, how long was it watched, was it liked. At serving time the model predicts those outcomes for new candidates, and the system sorts by a score built from the predictions. Everything the model "wants" comes from the labels and the scoring formula. It has no idea what the product is for.

An analogy: paying a sales team on commission. If you pay per sale, they sell, including to customers who will return the product next week. If you pay per sale net of returns, they become more careful. If you pay on customer satisfaction scores, some will start coaching customers on how to fill in the survey. Each pay scheme is a proxy for "build lasting customer relationships", and each is exploited in its own way. The fix in sales is the same as in ML: combine several measures, watch for gaming, and change the scheme when it stops tracking the real goal.

Where the analogy breaks: salespeople understand the intent behind their targets and many will honour it. A model has no intent to honour. It will exploit any regularity that raises its objective, including ones no human would think of, such as learning that videos uploaded at certain times by certain channels have inflated watch time because of autoplay. Models are more literal optimisers than people, which makes the objective more important, not less.

The core move of this lesson is to treat the chain explicitly. You decide the product goal and online metric (ps2). You choose labels that are as close to them as you can observe at useful volume. You combine several predicted labels into a score whose weights express what matters. You add rules the model should not have to learn, such as safety filters and diversity requirements. And you check, online, that optimising the score moves the product metric. When it does not, the fix is almost always further up the chain than the model.

A reader who stops here has the right picture: labels are proxies, every proxy has a gap, a single proxy is easy to exploit, and a production objective is a deliberate combination of several proxies plus constraints, judged online. The rest of the lesson makes each step concrete with numbers.

One more framing helps before the details. There are three distinct questions hiding in "what should the model optimise?", and they have different owners. What is valuable is a product question, answered with user research and the north-star metric. What can we observe, at what volume and delay is a data question, answered by the logging and the label pipeline. How should the observable signals be combined is a modelling and experimentation question, answered with calibrated heads, weights and online tests. Weak objectives usually come from answering only the second question ("we have click logs, so we predict clicks") and treating the first and third as settled.

It also helps to know what the model actually sees at training time, because that is where many objective problems hide. Each training row is one impression: the features of the user, the item and the context at the moment it was shown, plus the logged outcome. Impressions that were never shown have no row. Outcomes that happen later (the user came back tomorrow, the purchase was refunded next week) are only present if someone joined them onto the row, which requires a pipeline that waits for them. So the practical question "what can the model optimise?" is often answered by "what does the label pipeline join onto each impression, and how long does it wait?". If the answer is "clicks within 30 seconds", that is the objective, whatever the design document says.
body:
1. The labels you can actually observe

For a content or commerce product, the outcomes you can log after an impression form a ladder, from dense and fast but far from value, to sparse and slow but close to it:

LabelTypical frequencyDelayMain distortion
Click or tapHigh (a few per 100 impressions)SecondsRewards thumbnails, titles, curiosity
Dwell or watch timeHigh (every click has one)MinutesRewards length, autoplay, compulsion
Completion (watched to the end, read to the end)MediumMinutesRewards short items
Like, save, followLow (a few per 1,000)MinutesBiased towards habitual likers and some content types
Share, commentVery lowMinutes to hoursRewards outrage and controversy as well as delight
Purchase, subscriptionVery lowHours to weeksSparse; attribution across many impressions is hard
Explicit negative (hide, "not interested", report)LowSecondsOnly the most annoyed users bother
Survey ratingVery low (a sample)MinutesWho responds is not random; small samples
Return next weekPer user, not per itemDaysHard to attribute to individual items

Two forces pull in opposite directions. Dense, fast labels give the model lots of training data and quick feedback, which is why first models nearly always use clicks. Sparse, slow labels sit closer to value but give little data and can be impossible to attribute to a single impression: a user returned next week because of the whole experience, not one video. Every production objective is a compromise between these forces.

All of these labels are also shaped by what the system chose to show (rec10). Items shown at the top are clicked more because of their position; items never shown have no labels at all. A model trained on these logs partly learns the old ranking's preferences. This matters for objectives because a label that seems to measure "user preference" also measures "what we showed".

2. The proxy gap, worked with numbers

Consider three candidate videos for one slot in a feed. Each has a predicted click probability, an average watch time for people who click, and the share of viewers who would rate it four or five stars in a survey.

VideoP(click)Watch if clickedRated 4-5 starsExpected watch per impressionExpected valued watch
A: shocking thumbnail, little content0.1020 s10%2 s0.2 s
B: clear 7-minute tutorial0.04400 s80%16 s12.8 s
C: 40-minute compilation0.06600 s30%36 s10.8 s

Expected watch per impression is P(click) × watch if clicked: 0.10 × 20 = 2, 0.04 × 400 = 16, 0.06 × 600 = 36 seconds. Expected valued watch weights that by the share of viewers who rate it highly: 2 × 0.1 = 0.2, 16 × 0.8 = 12.8, 36 × 0.3 = 10.8 seconds.

A click objective picks A. A watch-time objective picks C, by a wide margin. A valued-watch objective picks B. Same candidates, same predictions, three different winners. And the gap compounds: a feed ranked by clicks shows A-like videos all day, which teaches creators to make A-like videos, which changes tomorrow's candidates. The choice of objective shapes not just one ranking but what content exists on the platform.

3. Multi-objective scores: the value model

Because no single label equals value, most production rankers predict several outcomes and combine them. A multi-task model has shared layers and a separate output head for each outcome (rec6): P(click), expected watch time, P(like), P(share), P(not interested). The heads are combined by a value model, usually a weighted sum:

score = w_click·P(click) + w_watch·E[watch minutes] + w_like·P(like) + w_share·P(share) − w_neg·P(not interested)

The weights express how much each outcome is worth relative to the others. They are a product decision, not something the model learns. Changing them changes the ranking without retraining anything, which makes them a powerful and dangerous lever.

Worked example with three candidates and two weight settings:

CandidateP(click)E[watch] minP(like)P(share)P(not int.)Score, watch-heavyScore, satisfaction-heavy
X0.120.50.0100.0020.0300.09−0.55
Y0.051.50.0400.0100.0051.751.80
Z0.082.20.0150.0030.0201.9850.80

The watch-heavy weights are w_click = 1, w_watch = 1 per minute, w_like = 5, w_share = 10, w_neg = 20. For Z: 0.08 + 2.2 + 5 × 0.015 + 10 × 0.003 − 20 × 0.02 = 0.08 + 2.2 + 0.075 + 0.03 − 0.4 = 1.985. The satisfaction-heavy weights are w_click = 1, w_watch = 0.5, w_like = 20, w_share = 40, w_neg = 40. For Y: 0.05 + 0.75 + 0.8 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 1.80; for Z: 0.08 + 1.1 + 0.3 + 0.12 − 0.8 = 0.80. Under the first setting Z ranks first; under the second, Y does. Nothing about the model changed.

A value model is only as good as its inputs' calibration: whether a predicted 0.04 like probability really means about 4 in 100 viewers like it (ml7). Because the score adds predictions, a head that over-predicts by a factor of two after a retrain silently doubles that outcome's weight. Ranking metrics such as AUC do not detect this, because they only care about order within a head. Teams that use value models check each head's calibration after every retrain, overall and in major segments.

4. Setting the weights

There are three sources of evidence for weights, usually used together.

Value per event. Where an outcome has a known business value, use it. Ads rankers do this naturally: expected revenue is P(click) × bid. For consumer engagement, direct values are rarer, but some exist, for example the estimated contribution of a follow to future sessions.

Regression on a satisfaction signal. Take a sample of impressions where users answered a satisfaction survey, and regress the survey score on the observed events. If the regression says a like adds 1.2 points of satisfaction, a share 1.5, each minute of watching 0.08 (up to a cap), and a "not interested" click subtracts 2.0, those coefficients suggest relative weights. Survey samples are small and biased, so treat the result as a starting point, not an answer.

Online tuning. Run experiments with several weight settings and pick the one that best moves the long-term online metric (next-week return, survey satisfaction) within guardrails. This is the final arbiter, because it measures the effect of the whole ranking on users. It is slow (each setting needs an experiment arm) and noisy, so teams usually tune only a few weights at a time.

Whatever the method, weights need an owner, a written rationale and a review schedule. They drift out of date when the model's heads change, when the product adds a new surface, or when user behaviour shifts.

5. Goodhart's law in four forms

Goodhart's law began as an economist's observation about monetary policy (Charles Goodhart, 1975) and is usually quoted in the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern's general phrasing: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." For ML objectives it is the central hazard. Manheim and Garrabrant (2018) distinguish four mechanisms, and each has a ranking example.

Regressional. The proxy is the goal plus noise. When you select the items with the highest proxy, you also select items with lucky noise, so the goal improves less than the proxy suggests. In ranking: the top-predicted items have prediction errors that are, on average, positive; realised engagement on the top slots is lower than predicted. This is mild and unavoidable; it is why offline gains shrink online.

Extremal. The proxy tracks the goal in the normal range of the data but not at the extremes an optimiser pushes towards. Watch time tracks value for videos between two and twenty minutes; at ten-hour compilations, it tracks compulsion. A model trained on normal data and asked to maximise will drift into exactly the region where the relationship breaks.

Causal. The proxy correlates with the goal because both are caused by something else, so intervening on the proxy does not move the goal. Users who share are happy, but adding share prompts raises shares without making anyone happier: sharing was a symptom of satisfaction, not its cause.

Adversarial. Other agents learn what the system rewards and produce inputs that trigger it. Creators adopt the thumbnail style the ranker rewards; sellers stuff keywords into listings; spammers learn which phrases pass the filter. This form only appears after launch, because it requires people to adapt to the system.

The practical defences map onto the four: expect regressional shrinkage and do not over-interpret offline gains; cap or transform proxies at extremes (cap watch-time credit per video); prefer labels that are causes of value, validated by experiments; and monitor content and supply-side changes after launch.

6. Ecosystem objectives: constraints and policy layers

Some goals do not belong to any single impression. Creator health (do new and small creators get enough exposure to keep uploading?), diversity of topics, freshness, and fairness of exposure all describe the whole ranking or the whole platform. Adding them as another weight in the value model is possible but awkward: the weight's effect varies as other predictions shift, and it is hard to audit.

The usual alternative is a constraint or a policy layer applied after scoring (rec12): "at least 10% of slots go to creators with under 1,000 followers", "no more than two videos from the same channel in the top ten", "items flagged by the safety classifier are removed regardless of score". Google's Rules of Machine Learning recommends a similar separation in Rule 15: keep spam filtering and quality ranking in a policy layer rather than mixing them into one model. Constraints are easy to explain, easy to audit, and their cost can be measured by experiment (how much does the primary metric fall when the new-creator floor rises from 5% to 10%?).

7. Delayed outcomes and surrogate labels

The outcomes that matter most, such as 90-day retention, lifetime value and loan repayment, arrive too late to train on directly; by the time you have the label, the world has changed. Teams use surrogate labels: short-term outcomes that predict the long-term one, such as 7-day return or first-week activity. Choosing a surrogate is exactly the proxy-validation problem from ps2: the surrogate must move with the long-term outcome across interventions, not just correlate with it across users.

A more sophisticated approach combines several short-term outcomes into a predicted long-term value, trained on historical users whose long-term outcomes are now known, and uses that prediction as the label. It reduces delay at the cost of one more model whose errors become the ranker's objective.

8. A procedure for choosing the objective

Pulling it together, for a new ranking or prediction system:

  1. Write the product goal and the online metric that will judge the launch (ps2).
  2. List observable labels with their frequency, delay and distortion; pick a primary label dense enough to learn from and a few secondary labels that catch its distortion (watch time to correct clicks, negative feedback to correct watch time).
  3. Train heads for each, check calibration, and combine in a simple value model with documented weights.
  4. Put platform-level goals (safety, diversity, creator exposure) in a policy layer as constraints.
  5. Run an online experiment judged on the product metric, with counter-metrics for each label's distortion.
  6. When offline gains stop translating into online gains, revisit the labels and weights before the model architecture, as Rule 38 of Rules of ML puts it: "don't waste time on new features if unaligned objectives have become the issue".

9. Worked back-chain: from next-week return to a ranking objective

Interviewers often give you the product metric and ask you to design the objective. Here is the reasoning, made explicit, for a short-video feed whose launch metric is next-week return rate (the share of this week's active users who are active next week).

First, ask what per-impression outcomes plausibly cause users to come back. Candidate causes: they found something they enjoyed (watch time on content they rate highly), they found something to follow (follows of new creators, which create a reason to return), and they did not have a bad experience (absence of "not interested" and reports). Candidate symptoms that do not cause return: clicks on their own, and very long sessions late at night that users later regret.

Second, check which outcomes you can log at volume. Clicks and watch time, yes. Follows and "not interested", at lower volume. Ratings, only from a survey sample, so you would predict them with a satisfaction model trained on survey responses.

Third, validate with history. Using, say, 40 past ranking experiments, regress each experiment's effect on next-week return against its effects on average watch time, follows per user, "not interested" rate and predicted satisfaction. Suppose watch time explains little once satisfaction is included, while follows and "not interested" explain a lot. That tells you which heads deserve weight.

Fourth, compose: score = P(click) × E[watch | click] × predicted satisfaction + w_follow × P(follow) − w_neg × P(not interested), with watch-time credit capped per video so ten-hour compilations cannot dominate. Fifth, test the composed objective against the current one with next-week return as the primary metric, and expect raw watch time to fall a little; decide in advance that this is acceptable. That is the full translation, and saying these five steps out loud is a strong answer to "what would your model optimise?".

10. Checking an objective before you launch it

Online experiments are the final test, but they are slow and expensive, so teams check a new objective offline first. Three checks are cheap and catch most surprises.

Look at what it ranks first. Re-rank a sample of real candidate sets with the new objective and read the top results. If the top ten for a typical user are all 40-minute compilations, you have found an extremal problem without an experiment. This sounds unscientific, but it catches glaring objective bugs quickly. Rule 23 of Rules of ML ("you are not a typical end user") is the caveat: your taste is not your users', so reading results complements measurement rather than replacing it.

Compare distributions. For the old and new objectives, compare the distribution of the top-k items by length, age, creator size, content category and predicted negative feedback. A new objective that shifts exposure heavily toward one category or away from small creators should be a conscious choice, not a surprise found in a launch review.

Estimate the effect counterfactually. With logs from a system that sometimes explored (showed items in randomised positions), you can estimate how the new ranking would have performed on the old traffic by reweighting logged outcomes (inverse propensity weighting, rec10). These estimates are noisy and only cover outcomes you logged, but they flag objectives that would obviously lose on a guardrail.

11. The same translation outside feeds

Fraud detection. The product goal is to stop fraud without blocking good customers. The label is usually "charged back within 90 days", which arrives late and only for transactions that were allowed (blocked ones have no outcome). The objective is not "maximise accuracy" but "minimise expected cost": each false block costs the lost margin plus the chance the customer leaves, and each missed fraud costs the chargeback plus fees. Writing the objective as cost lets you pick a threshold that is a product decision with a number on it, which hd4 develops.

ETA (estimated time of arrival) prediction. Training to minimise mean absolute error treats one minute early and one minute late the same, but riders are more upset by late arrivals than early ones. An asymmetric loss that penalises under-prediction more (hd20 describes one used in production) is a product decision encoded in the loss function.

LLM assistants. Thumbs-up rate is the dense, fast label, and it rewards answers that feel good: confident, agreeable, long. Task completion (did the user's problem get solved, did they not have to ask again) is the value. The objective for evaluating prompts or fine-tunes should weight task completion and correctness, with thumbs-up as a secondary signal and sycophancy checks as counter-metrics (ps10 and sf3).
deep:
Objective, metric and loss are three different things

Interviewers sometimes test whether you separate them. The product metric is what the launch is judged on (next-week return). The objective is what the ranking maximises (the value-model score). The loss is what each head minimises during training (log loss for P(click), a regression loss for watch time). A model can minimise its loss perfectly and still rank badly if the objective is wrong; an objective can be right and still fail if a head's loss rewards the wrong thing (for example, mean squared error on raw watch time lets a few hour-long sessions dominate training). Being explicit about all three, and about which one failed when something goes wrong, is a senior signal.

Predicting expected value directly

One elegant trick avoids a separate watch-time head. YouTube's 2016 recommendation paper (Covington, Adams and Sargin) describes training the ranking model with weighted logistic regression: clicked impressions are positives weighted by their watch time, unclicked impressions are negatives with weight one. The learned odds then approximate expected watch time per impression, so ranking by the model's output ranks by expected watch time. It is a clean way to optimise a continuous value with a classification model, and it shows how the choice of example weights is itself an objective choice: weight positives by satisfaction-adjusted watch time, and the same machinery optimises something different.

Weighted sums versus constrained optimisation

A weighted sum assumes outcomes are substitutes at a fixed rate: one share is worth exactly ten likes everywhere. Often the real preference is a threshold: "maximise watch time as long as negative-feedback rate stays below 1%". That is a constrained optimisation problem, and the standard technique (Lagrange multipliers, math11) turns the constraint into a weight that is adjusted until the constraint just holds. In practice teams approximate it by tuning the negative-feedback weight until the guardrail is met. Saying "this is really a constraint, and the weight is its multiplier" shows you understand why the weights are not arbitrary.

The objective shapes the data it learns from

A ranker trained on its own logs creates a feedback loop: what it promotes gets more labels, so it learns more about it and promotes it more (rec10). The objective decides what enters that loop. A click objective fills the logs with clicks on clickbait, so the next model is even better at clickbait. Exploration (showing some items for learning rather than for score), counterfactual weighting of logged data, and holding out a small randomly ranked slice are the standard counters. For objective design the lesson is that a bad objective gets worse over retrains, not just stays bad.

Reward models in LLM training are the same problem

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF, lm6) trains a reward model on human comparisons of responses, then optimises a language model to score highly on it. The reward model is a proxy for "what people want", and pushing hard against it produces reward hacking: longer answers, more flattering answers, confident tone (sf3 covers sycophancy). The mitigations rhyme with recommender practice: a penalty for drifting far from a reference model (Kullback-Leibler regularisation, the analogue of a constraint), several reward signals rather than one, and evaluation on fresh human judgements rather than on the reward model itself. An AI engineer who can draw the parallel between a feed's value model and an LLM's reward model is showing exactly the transferable judgement senior roles want.

Who should own the weights

In many organisations the value-model weights live in a config file edited by whichever engineer is tuning the ranker this quarter. That is a governance gap: the weights decide what millions of users see and what creators are rewarded for. Mature teams treat them like a product specification: changes go through review, are tested in experiments, and are recorded with the reason and the measured effect. In an interview, mentioning that weight changes need the same launch discipline as model changes is a small point that signals experience.

User agency as part of the objective

Explicit controls, such as "not interested", "show fewer like this", topic follows and the ability to reset recommendations, provide labels that are closer to intent than any implicit signal, and they give users a way to correct the system when it drifts. YouTube's 2021 post lists dislikes alongside likes and shares as signals, and notes that how much each signal matters depends on the individual user. Designing for explicit feedback is therefore both a product feature and an objective-quality investment.

Diminishing returns and capping

Most outcomes have diminishing value: the tenth minute of a video is worth less than the first, and the fifth follow of the day less than the first. A linear weight on raw watch time ignores this and hands the largest rewards to the longest items, which is the extremal failure in another form. Common fixes are capping the credit per item (count watch time up to five minutes), using a concave transform such as the logarithm of watch time, or crediting completion of a fraction rather than raw minutes. Each choice changes which content the system favours, so it belongs in the documented objective, not in a feature engineer's preprocessing script.
prod:
The real case: YouTube's changing objective

In September 2021, YouTube's vice president (VP) of engineering, Cristos Goodrow, published a first-party account of the signals behind its recommendations. Its history is a compact version of this whole lesson. Clicks came first, but the post says YouTube "learned back in 2011 that clicking on a video doesn't mean you actually watched it", using the example of someone searching for Wimbledon highlights who clicks on videos whose thumbnails suggest match footage but which turn out to be people talking about the match.

So YouTube "added in watchtime in 2012". The post is candid about the cost: "When we first incorporated watchtime into recommendations, we saw an immediate 20% drop in views. But we believed that it was more important for us to deliver more value to viewers." That is a launch decision that accepted a large loss on one metric (views, a click-like measure) for a better objective.

Then the post acknowledges the next gap: "not all watchtime is equal". The author describes staying up late watching random videos instead of learning something, and says YouTube did not want viewers regretting the time they spent. Its response was to measure "valued watchtime", time spent watching a video that you consider valuable, through surveys asking viewers to rate videos from one to five stars, with follow-up questions about why. Only highly rated videos count as valued watchtime. Because few people answer surveys, YouTube trained a model to predict survey responses for everyone, and checks it by holding back some survey responses from training and comparing predictions with them. The post also lists sharing, likes and dislikes as signals, with their importance depending on the individual user.

The engineering lessons are general. Objectives evolve as each proxy's gap becomes visible. Moving to a better objective can cost a lot on the old metric, and someone has to be willing to accept that. And survey-based satisfaction becomes usable at scale only through a predictive model, whose own accuracy must then be monitored like any other.

Failure modes in production

Silent head miscalibration. A retrain changes the like head's calibration; items with many predicted likes jump up the ranking; engagement shifts in ways nobody intended. Symptom: the distribution of value-model scores shifts after a retrain while no weight changed. Defence: calibration checks per head as a deployment gate.

Weight changes without experiments. An engineer bumps the share weight to "encourage virality" in a config change. Shares rise; so do reports of misleading content. Symptom: counter-metrics move on a day with no model release. Defence: weights live in reviewed config, and changes go through the experiment platform.

Label definition drift. The client app changes when it logs "watched", for example after autoplay starts rather than after the user taps. Watch-time labels inflate for autoplayed items, and the model learns to favour items that autoplay well. Defence: data-quality metrics on labels per client version, and label definitions owned like metric definitions.

Supply-side adaptation. Months after a successful launch, creators or sellers adapt to the objective, and content quality shifts. Symptom: the share of new content matching a pattern the ranker likes rises steadily. Defence: monitor the supply side (content types, title styles, length distributions), not just user metrics.

Debugging an objective problem

When a launch improves the label but not the product metric, a systematic approach saves weeks. First, confirm the experiment is valid (sample ratio, logging, exposure) before blaming the objective. Second, check the counter-metrics for each label's known distortion: abandoned starts for clicks, negative feedback and regret surveys for watch time. Third, compare the content that gained exposure with the content that lost it, by category, length, creator size and age; objective problems usually show up as a systematic shift. Fourth, look at calibration of each head in the treatment; a miscalibrated head changes the effective weights. Fifth, segment the product-metric effect by user type: new users often react differently from heavy users. Only after these checks is it worth changing the model itself.
myths: If you choose the right label, the model will optimise the product goal.

No single observable label is the product goal. Clicks, watch time, likes and purchases are each a partial, biased view of value, and a model optimises the label's quirks along with its signal. In practice teams combine several predicted outcomes into one score, add constraints the model cannot learn from labels (diversity, policy), and check the result online against the product metric.
Watch time is a better objective than clicks, so optimising it fixes clickbait.

It fixes one failure and introduces another. YouTube reports that adding watch time in 2012 caused an immediate 20% drop in views, a price it chose to pay because clicks did not mean people watched. But YouTube also says not all watch time is equal: some of it is time people regret. Watch time rewards long, compulsive content much as clicks reward thumbnails, which is why it later added survey-based 'valued watchtime'.
Goodhart's law means metrics are useless once you optimise them.

It means the relationship between a metric and the goal weakens under optimisation pressure, especially at the extremes and when someone can game it. The practical response is not to stop measuring but to use several partially independent signals, cap or constrain the easily gamed ones, re-validate proxies against the goal periodically, and watch counter-metrics.
Weights in a multi-objective score should be learned by the model.

The model learns to predict each outcome; the weights that combine those predictions express what the business values, which is a product decision. They can be informed by data (regressing survey satisfaction on predicted events, or tuning weights in online experiments), but someone must own them, document them, and re-test them when the product changes.
A better offline metric on the training label means a better product.

Only if the label tracks the product goal in the region the model operates. A model can get much better at predicting clicks on clickbait, raising offline AUC, while the product gets worse. Offline metrics tell you the model learned its label; only online product metrics tell you the label was the right one.
lab:
Goal: see three objectives pick different items, and trace the trade-off between watch time and satisfaction as a weight changes. About 15 minutes; Python 3.12 standard library.

  1. Save as objectives.py and run it:
import random
random.seed(7)
items = []
for i in range(5000):
    quality = random.random()             # hidden true value, 0..1
    bait = random.random()                # how clickbaity the packaging is
    length = random.choice([1, 3, 8, 20, 45])   # minutes
    p_click = 0.02 + 0.08 * bait + 0.02 * quality
    watch = length * (0.15 + 0.6 * quality) * (1 - 0.5 * bait)  # minutes if clicked
    p_happy = min(1.0, 0.05 + 0.85 * quality - 0.3 * bait + 0.1 * random.random())
    items.append((p_click, p_click * watch, p_click * watch * max(p_happy, 0), quality))

def top(key, k=50):
    best = sorted(items, key=key, reverse=True)[:k]
    n = len(best)
    return [round(sum(x[j] for x in best) / n, 3) for j in range(4)]

print("objective        p_click  E[watch]  E[valued]  quality")
for name, key in [("click", lambda x: x[0]), ("watch", lambda x: x[1]), ("valued", lambda x: x[2])]:
    print(f"{name:15}", top(key))
for lam in [0, 0.5, 1, 2, 5]:
    r = top(lambda x: x[1] + lam * x[2])
    print(f"watch + {lam} * valued -> E[watch] {r[1]}, E[valued] {r[2]}, quality {r[3]}")

What to look for: the click objective should give the highest average click probability and the lowest true quality; the watch objective the highest expected watch time, with quality in between; the valued objective the highest quality. In the sweep, raising the weight on valued watch time should trade a little expected watch time for noticeably higher quality, an example of a trade-off curve. Then change the generator so that bait also raises watch (autoplay-style compulsion) and see how much worse the watch objective becomes. Write two sentences on which objective you would ship first and what counter-metric you would watch.
recap: A model optimises exactly the label and loss it is given, so choosing them is a product decision made by engineers.
Observable labels such as clicks, dwell time, completion, likes, shares, purchases and survey answers trade off density, delay, noise and distance from true value; no single one equals value.
The proxy gap can be worked with numbers: ranking by click probability, by expected watch time and by expected valued watch time can pick three different items from the same three candidates.
Most production rankers predict several outcomes with separate heads and combine them in a value model, score = sum of weight × predicted outcome, which requires calibrated predictions.
Weights express business value and can be set from value per event, from regressions of survey satisfaction on events, or by online tuning, but they need an owner and periodic re-testing.
Goodhart's law says a measure that becomes a target loses its connection to the goal; the four mechanisms are regressional, extremal, causal and adversarial.
Ecosystem objectives, such as exposure for new creators, are usually better expressed as constraints or a separate re-ranking layer than as one more weight in the score.

YouTube moved from clicks to watch time in 2012, accepting an immediate 20% drop in views, then added 'valued watchtime' from 1-5 star surveys, using a model trained on survey answers to predict satisfaction for everyone.
The test of an objective is online: if offline gains on the label do not move the product metric, change the objective rather than the model.
glossary: AUC
Area under the ROC curve: how often a model ranks a random positive above a random negative; it ignores calibration (ml7).
Calibration
A property of predicted probabilities: among items predicted at 0.2, about 20% have the outcome. Needed whenever predictions are added or multiplied together.
Constraint
A requirement the ranking must satisfy regardless of score, such as at least 10% of slots for new creators, as opposed to a weight traded off against other goals.
Dwell time
How long a user stays on an item after opening it; used as a quality signal on the assumption that longer means more valuable.
Extremal Goodhart
The failure where a proxy that tracks the goal in the normal range stops tracking it at the extreme values an optimiser pushes towards.
Goodhart's law
The observation that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure, because optimisation exploits the gap between measure and goal.
Inverse propensity weighting
Reweighting logged outcomes by one over the probability the old system showed that item in that position, to estimate how a different ranking would have performed (rec10).
Label
The observed outcome a supervised model is trained to predict, such as whether an impression was clicked.
LLM
Large language model: a model trained on large amounts of text that generates text from a prompt.
Multi-task model
A model with shared layers and several output heads, each predicting a different outcome such as click, like or watch time.
Policy layer
Rules applied after model scoring (filters, caps, diversity and freshness requirements) that encode decisions the model should not learn from labels.
Proxy gap
The difference between what a label measures and the value the product wants; the source of most objective failures.
Regressional Goodhart
The failure where selecting on a noisy proxy picks items whose proxy is high partly because of noise, so the goal improves less than the proxy suggests.
Reward hacking
An optimiser finding a way to score highly on its objective without achieving the intended goal; the term comes from reinforcement learning and also applies to rankers and LLM training.
RLHF
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimising a language model against it (lm6).
Surrogate label
A short-term, observable outcome used in place of a long-term one that arrives too late to train on, such as 7-day return in place of 90-day retention.
Value model
The formula that combines a ranker's predicted outcomes into one score, typically a weighted sum, with weights expressing how much each outcome is worth.
Valued watchtime
YouTube's term for watch time on videos users rate highly in surveys; measured with 1-5 star surveys and predicted for everyone with a model.
Weighted logistic regression
Logistic regression in which each training example has a weight; with positives weighted by watch time, the learned odds approximate expected watch time, a trick YouTube's 2016 paper describes.
drill:
Objective design drill

Wayfare, a hypothetical travel-booking app, ranks hotels in search results by predicted click probability. Bookings per search are flat, but the share of bookings cancelled within 48 hours has risen from 6% to 9% since the ranker launched. Diagnose the likely objective problem and propose a new objective, with how you would set it and test it.

Answer

Diagnosis: a click objective rewards listings whose photos and headline prices attract clicks. A likely pattern is low headline prices that rise at checkout (fees) or flattering photos; users click, some book, then cancel when they see the real price or reviews. That is a proxy gap with an adversarial element: hotels learn what the ranker rewards.

New objective: predict several outcomes per impression: P(click), P(book | click), P(cancel within 48 h | book), and expected margin per booking. Score = P(click) × P(book | click) × (1 − P(cancel)) × margin, i.e. expected completed-booking value per impression, plus a small weight on P(click) to keep the model learning from dense data. Check calibration of each head, especially P(cancel), which is rarer.

Policy layer: rank on total price including mandatory fees, not headline price, as a rule rather than a learned feature, which removes the incentive to hide fees.

Test: experiment with the primary metric completed (non-cancelled) bookings per searching user over 2-3 weeks; guardrails: search latency, revenue per searching user, hotel-side metrics (bookings for small hotels); counter-metric: post-stay review score and cancellation rate. Expect clicks to fall, and decide in advance that a fall in clicks is acceptable if completed bookings rise, as YouTube accepted fewer views for more watch time.
qa: E
Why is choosing a model's training label a product decision?

Because the model will become very good at predicting and therefore promoting whatever the label rewards. If the label is a click, the system promotes things people click, including clickbait; if it is watch time, it promotes long content, including content people regret. The label is the operational definition of 'good' for the system, so it should be chosen from the product goal, not from what is easiest to log.
E
List some labels a feed ranker could train on and one weakness of each.

Click: dense and fast but rewards thumbnails and titles. Dwell or watch time: closer to engagement but rewards length and compulsive content. Like or share: closer to value but sparse and biased towards some users and content types. Purchase or subscription: close to business value but very sparse and delayed. Survey satisfaction: closest to value but rare, biased by who responds, and needs a model to scale.
E
State Goodhart's law and give an ML example.

When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. A recommender trained to maximise click-through learns that sensational thumbnails get clicks, so CTR rises while satisfaction falls; the measure (CTR) stopped tracking the goal (users finding things they value) once it was optimised.
M

Three candidate videos: A has click probability 0.10 and 20 seconds average watch after a click; B 0.04 and 400 seconds; C 0.06 and 600 seconds. 10%, 80% and 30% of their viewers respectively rate them 4 or 5 stars. Which would each objective rank first?

By click probability, A (0.10). By expected watch time per impression, C: A gives 0.10 × 20 = 2 s, B 0.04 × 400 = 16 s, C 0.06 × 600 = 36 s. By expected valued watch time (watch time from viewers who rate it highly), B: A 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 s, B 16 × 0.8 = 12.8 s, C 36 × 0.3 = 10.8 s. Three objectives, three winners, which is why the choice matters.

Follow-up: Which would you ship? — None alone: I would combine predicted click, watch time and a satisfaction signal in a value model, and decide the weights by online experiments measured on a long-term metric such as next-week return.
M
Why must predictions be calibrated before you combine them in a value model?

A value model adds weighted predictions, so each prediction's scale matters. If the like head systematically over-predicts by a factor of two after a retrain, items with high predicted likes jump up the ranking even though nothing about them changed. Ranking metrics like AUC ignore calibration, so a head can look fine offline and still distort the combined score; checking calibration per head and per segment after each retrain prevents this.
M
How would you set the weights in score = w1·p(click) + w2·E[watch] + w3·p(like) − w4·p(not interested)?

Start from value per event if it exists (ads revenue per click, subscription value), use a regression of survey satisfaction on the events to estimate relative worth, then tune online: run experiments that vary the weights and choose the setting that best moves the long-term product metric while respecting guardrails. Document the weights and who owns them, and re-tune when the product or the model heads change.

Follow-up: What if two weight settings tie on the primary metric? — Prefer the one with better guardrails and counter-metrics (fewer 'not interested', better survey scores), since it is less likely to be gaming.
M
What is a surrogate label and when do you need one?

A short-term outcome used in place of a long-term one that arrives too late to train on: 7-day return instead of 90-day retention, first-week repayment behaviour instead of loan default. You need it whenever the true outcome is delayed or sparse. The risk is that the model optimises the surrogate's quirks, so validate that interventions which move the surrogate also move the long-term outcome.
M
Why express creator diversity as a constraint rather than another weight?

A weight trades diversity against everything else continuously, so its effect varies as other predictions shift and it is hard to reason about. A constraint (at least 10% of slots for creators with under 1,000 followers) guarantees the outcome, is easy to audit, and can be tuned by experiment. Rules of ML similarly advises keeping policy concerns such as spam in a separate layer rather than inside the quality model.
M
What did YouTube change in its recommendation objective, and what did it cost?

According to YouTube's 2021 post by its VP of engineering, it learned in 2011 that clicks did not mean people watched, added watch time in 2012, and saw an immediate 20% drop in views, which it accepted for more value per viewer. Later it added valued watchtime: 1-5 star surveys, with a model trained on survey answers to predict satisfaction for everyone and held-back survey responses to check the model's accuracy.
H
Describe the four kinds of Goodhart failure and an example of each in a ranking system.

Regressional: picking the top items by a noisy predicted score selects items whose score is high partly by noise, so realised value is lower than predicted. Extremal: watch time tracks value for normal videos but not for ten-hour compilations the optimiser surfaces. Causal: users who share are happy, but forcing share prompts raises shares without raising happiness, because sharing was a symptom not a cause. Adversarial: creators learn what the ranker rewards and produce content that triggers it, such as misleading thumbnails.
Follow-up: Which is hardest to catch with offline evaluation? — Adversarial, because it appears only after the system is live and people adapt; offline data reflects behaviour under the old system.
H
Your new ranker improves predicted watch time by 6% offline and raises watch time 3% online, but 'not interested' clicks rise 8%. What do you do?

Treat it as a likely Goodhart failure: the model is finding watch time that users partly dislike. Segment to see where the not-interested rise is concentrated (content types, new versus heavy users), check satisfaction surveys in the experiment, and look at next-week return as the arbiter. Then add or up-weight a negative-feedback head or a satisfaction signal and rerun; I would not ship on watch time alone with a counter-metric up 8%.
H
How do LLM reward models relate to recommender objectives?

They are the same problem. In RLHF a reward model trained on human preference comparisons stands in for 'what people want', and the policy optimises it; push too hard and the policy finds outputs that score well but are worse (reward hacking, such as verbosity or sycophancy). Practitioners respond the way recommender teams do: a penalty that keeps the model close to a reference (KL regularisation, the analogue of a constraint), several reward signals, and evaluation on held-out human judgements rather than the reward model's own score.
H
When would you choose a simple, imperfect objective over a carefully composed one?

Early in a product, or for a first model, as Rules of ML advises: a simple, observable, attributable objective lets you build the pipeline, measure online, and learn where the proxy gap bites. A composed objective with many weights is hard to debug and invites arguments before there is data. I would move to a composite once the simple objective's failure modes are visible in counter-metrics and the team has experiments to set weights.
refs: Goodrow, On YouTube's recommendation system (YouTube Official Blog, 15 September 2021)
First-party account of the signals: clicks (2011 lesson), watch time added in 2012 with an immediate 20% drop in views, and survey-based valued watchtime predicted by a model.
Manheim & Garrabrant, Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law (2018)
Defines the regressional, extremal, causal and adversarial variants used in this lesson.
Zinkevich, Rules of Machine Learning (Google for Developers)
Rules 12-15 on choosing objectives and separating policy from quality ranking; Rule 38 on unaligned objectives; Rule 39 on launch decisions as proxies for long-term goals.
Covington, Adams & Sargin, Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations (RecSys 2016)
Describes ranking by expected watch time via weighted logistic regression (positives weighted by watch time); hd3 covers the architecture.
History of the law from Goodhart's 1975 monetary-policy remark to Strathern's general phrasing.

t: Diagnosing a metric change: data validity first, internal vs external causes, segmentation, funnel decomposition, mix shift and Simpson's paradox, with a worked investigation
sum: A method for 'DAU dropped 10%, why?': pin down the question, check the change is real and the data is valid, sort internal from external causes, segment to localise, decompose the funnel, separate mix shift from rate change (Simpson's paradox, with the Berkeley admissions data), and run a full worked investigation to a root cause.
prereq: ps2

Metric trees decompose a top-level metric multiplicatively; the share of a change explained by each factor is its log change over the total log change. Ratio metrics can move because their denominator changed.
math6
A change is only meaningful relative to normal variation; a confidence interval or a z-score compares an observed difference with the noise you would expect.
math1
Conditional probability: a rate within a group can differ from the overall rate, and the overall rate depends on how the population is split between groups.
why:
It is 9:10 on a Tuesday morning. A message lands in the team channel: "DAU down 10% yesterday?!" with a screenshot of a dashboard line falling off a cliff. Within twenty minutes there are four theories. The growth lead blames a competitor's launch. A product manager points at Monday's redesign of the home screen. Someone mentions that a marketing campaign ended on Sunday. An engineer suggests it might be the new notification throttling. Each theory has a champion, each champion starts pulling data to support it, and by lunchtime there are four half-finished analyses that disagree.

By the afternoon someone notices that the drop is entirely in one app version on one platform, that server-side traffic from that version fell far less than client-side events, and that the version's release notes include "migrated analytics library". Part of the "drop" is events that were never sent. The rest, it turns out, is real: the same release broke a login refresh, and some users were logged out. Neither the competitor, the redesign, the campaign nor the throttling had anything to do with it.

This is the normal shape of metric investigations that go badly: people start from causes they find plausible and look for confirming evidence, instead of starting from the data and narrowing down. The skill interviewers test with "DAU dropped 10%, why?" is not guessing the right cause. It is having a method that finds the cause quickly whatever it is, communicates progress clearly, and does not get fooled by measurement problems, coincidences or mix shifts.

This lesson gives that method. It covers pinning down the question; checking that the change is real and the data valid; separating internal from external causes; segmenting to localise the change, ranked by contribution; decomposing funnels; separating mix shift from rate change, including Simpson's paradox with the real 1973 Berkeley admissions numbers; and a complete worked investigation from alert to root cause with numbers at every step.
primer:
A metric change investigation starts with an observation ("this number moved") and ends with an explanation that is specific enough to act on ("Android version 8.4 broke login refresh for users whose token expired; it cost about 960,000 daily users; halt the rollout and ship the hotfix"). In between is a narrowing process: each step rules out large classes of explanation until one remains.

The best analogy is a mechanic diagnosing a car that "has lost power". A good mechanic does not start by replacing the part they suspect most. They first check whether the complaint is real and measured correctly: is the speedometer accurate, is the car carrying a heavy load, is it going uphill? Then they check the obvious external factors: was it a hot day, did the owner switch fuel? Then they localise: is the problem at all speeds or only when accelerating, in all gears or one? Then they follow the power path step by step from fuel to wheels to find where it is lost. Only then do they open the engine.

Where the analogy breaks: a car is one machine, while a metric aggregates millions of users who differ. A product metric can fall even though nothing broke for anyone, simply because the mix of users changed (more users from a group that naturally uses the product less). Cars do not have an equivalent of Simpson's paradox. That is why segmentation and mix analysis are central to product diagnosis in a way they are not to mechanics.

The order is the method. Clarifying first prevents investigating the wrong question. Checking reality and data validity next prevents investigating a measurement artefact, which is the cheapest class of cause to rule out and among the most common. The timeline gives a list of candidate causes. Segmentation and funnel decomposition narrow the change to a place and a step, which usually points at one candidate. Mix analysis checks that the change is not just a reshuffling of who is in the data. Confirmation turns a correlation into a cause.

A reader who stops here has the essential method: clarify, check it is real, check the data, list what changed, localise by segment and step, separate mix from rate, confirm, act. The body works through each step with numbers and then runs a full investigation.

One habit makes the method work under pressure: write the hypotheses down as a list with a status for each (open, ruled out, confirmed) and update it as you go. It keeps a group investigation from splitting into competing analyses, it makes progress visible to the people waiting for an answer, and in an interview it shows the interviewer exactly how you are narrowing the space. "Ruled out: competitor launch (drop is only on Android, competitor affects all platforms); open: Android release 8.4, logging change" is the kind of sentence that signals method.

It also helps to recognise the two shapes a metric change can take, because they point to different families of cause. A step change, where the metric is normal one day and different the next, almost always has a discrete cause with a timestamp: a release, a configuration change, an outage, a logging change, a holiday. The investigation is a search for that timestamp. A trend change, where the metric drifts over weeks, almost never has a single timestamp; it comes from something accumulating, such as weaker new-user retention, a slow shift in where users come from, or a competitor gradually taking share. The investigation is a decomposition of flows over time. Saying which shape you are looking at in the first two minutes of an interview, and why it changes your plan, is an easy way to show method.
body:
1. Pin down the question

"DAU dropped 10%" is not yet a question you can investigate. Ask five things first.

What exactly is the metric? DAU, daily active users, can mean users who opened the app, users who were logged in, or users who did the core action. It can be counted by account or by device, in UTC or local time. Different definitions react differently to different causes: a login bug hits "logged-in active" but not "app opened".

How big, compared with what? Down 10% versus yesterday is meaningless if yesterday was a Sunday and the product is used for work. Down 10% versus the same weekday last week (week-over-week) removes the weekly cycle. Down 10% versus a forecast takes trend and seasonality into account.

Since when, and how fast? A step change on one day points to a discrete event: a release, an outage, a logging change. A gradual slide over weeks points to something that accumulates: worse retention, slower acquisition, a competitor.

Is it one metric or many? If DAU, sessions, orders and revenue all fell together, something affected the whole product or its measurement. If DAU fell but orders did not, either the lost users were low-value or DAU's measurement changed.

Who noticed, and how? An automated alert, an executive reading a dashboard, a support spike. Support tickets mentioning a specific error are gold.

In an interview, ask two or three of these, state assumptions for the rest, and say them back: "So daily logged-in users, measured in UTC, fell from about 10.0 million to 9.0 million on Monday versus the previous Monday, suddenly, and other metrics also dipped. I'll start by checking whether that is outside normal variation and whether the data is complete."

2. Is the change real?

Metrics wobble. A 10% move only means something relative to normal variation. If Monday DAU over the last twelve weeks ranged between 9.8 and 10.2 million, the week-over-week change has a typical spread of about ±1.5%, and a 10% drop is several times that range: real. If the same metric for a small product swings ±12% week to week, a 10% drop is unremarkable.

The quick calculation: take the last 8-12 week-over-week changes for the same weekday, compute their standard deviation, and express today's change in those units. A change of more than three standard deviations is very unlikely to be noise. This is the same logic as the z-test in math6, applied to a time series rather than an experiment.

Seasonality, regular patterns such as weekly cycles, holidays and school terms, is the next suspect. Compare with the same period last year: if DAU also dipped 8% in the same week last year because of a national holiday or the start of school holidays, the current drop is probably seasonal. Some seasonal events move dates from year to year (Easter, Lunar New Year, Ramadan, Diwali), so compare with the event, not just the calendar date. If the team has a forecasting model with weekly and yearly components, its prediction interval is the natural yardstick.

3. Is the data valid?

This step is where experienced investigators save the most time. Before asking what users did differently, ask whether the measurement changed. Common measurement causes:

  • Late or partial data. Events from mobile clients that were offline arrive hours later. A pipeline job that failed for one region leaves a partition empty. Yesterday's value computed at 6 a.m. is too low and climbs during the day. Check data completeness: events per hour by source, partition row counts, and whether the value still changes when recomputed.
  • Logging changes. A client release migrates the analytics library, renames an event, or changes when an event fires. The drop is then confined to that client version. Microsoft's "dirty dozen" paper calls a related problem telemetry loss bias: client events can be lost, and if a change affects loss rates, metrics move without behaviour changing. They suggest comparing client events with corresponding server events (Skype's client and server "call" events) or using event sequence numbers to estimate loss.
  • Definition and processing changes. A new bot filter, a deduplication fix, a change in what counts as "active", a time-zone change in the pipeline. Check the data platform's change log.
  • Upstream outages. If the logging service itself was down, user activity happened but was not recorded.

The most powerful single check is corroboration with an independent source. Client-side analytics and server-side request logs are produced by different code. If client events fell 10% but server requests fell 1%, most of the drop is measurement. If both fell 10%, users really did less. In the worked investigation below, this check splits the drop into a measurement part and a real part.

4. Build a timeline: internal and external causes

Once the drop is real and the data trusted, list what changed around the time it started. Split the list in two.

Internal causes are changes the company made: client and server releases (including staged rollouts), experiments started or ramped, configuration and feature-flag changes, marketing changes (a campaign ending, a budget cut, an ad account suspended), pricing changes, notification or email volume changes, outages and incidents, and partner changes (a payment provider switch, a new app-store listing).

External causes are outside the company's control: holidays and seasonal events, weather, major news or sports events, competitor launches or promotions, platform changes (an operating-system update, a browser change, an app-store ranking algorithm change, a change in how a search engine ranks your pages), regulation, and outages at providers you depend on.

Put both on a timeline next to the metric. Internal changes are easy to list if the company annotates dashboards with deployments and experiments; if not, building that list is the first task. External causes are harder to enumerate, but two tests help: does the drop appear in a whole region or market (external events tend to be geographic), and do industry-wide signals (app-store rankings, search trends, competitor traffic estimates) move too?

5. Segment to localise the change

Segmentation asks where the change happened. Split the metric by the dimensions most likely to align with causes: platform (iOS, Android, web), app version, country or region, new versus returning users, acquisition channel or traffic source, device type, and user tenure. A release affects one platform and version; an outage affects a region or a data centre; a campaign ending affects one channel; a holiday affects one country.

The key discipline is to rank segments by contribution to the absolute change, not by percentage change. Contribution = the segment's change in absolute terms, divided by the total change. Here is the worked example for the investigation below (all figures in millions of DAU, Monday versus previous Monday):

PlatformLast MondayThis MondayChange% changeContribution
iOS4.204.17−0.03−0.7%3%
Android4.003.05−0.95−23.8%95%
Web1.801.78−0.02−1.1%2%
Total10.009.00−1.00−10.0%100%

Android explains 95% of the drop. Now segment Android by app version:

Android versionLast MondayThis MondayChangeContribution to Android drop
8.3 and older4.001.60−2.40—
8.4 (new, rolled out Monday to 60%)0.001.45+1.45—

Version tables need care, because users move between versions as a rollout proceeds: 8.3's apparent drop is mostly users upgrading. The right comparison is users on 8.4 versus users who stayed on 8.3, as a rate: of the 2.4 million users who would have been active on Android and received 8.4, how many were active? About 1.45 million, a 40% shortfall. Of the 1.6 million who stayed on 8.3, about 1.6 million were active, as expected. The drop is entirely in users who received 8.4. (This shortfall is measured with client-side events, so it still mixes real behaviour with any measurement loss; the next step separates them.)

Two cautions. First, the multiple-comparisons trap: with dozens of dimensions and hundreds of values, some slice will look extreme by chance, so start from likely dimensions and require the slice to explain a large share of the change. Second, segment shares themselves can move, which is the mix problem in section 7.

6. Decompose the funnel

Segmentation tells you where; funnel decomposition tells you which step. A funnel is a sequence of steps users pass through, with a conversion rate at each. For "logged-in daily active" on Android, a simplified funnel is: app opened → session token valid or refreshed → home screen loaded → active (any core action). Because the client-side events are under suspicion, build this funnel from server-side logs (app-open pings, authentication results, API calls). Per 100 Android users on 8.4 who opened the app on Monday, compared with 8.3:

Step8.3 (per 100 opens)8.4 (per 100 opens)Step rate 8.3Step rate 8.4
App opened100100——
Logged in (token valid or refreshed)977097%70%
Home loaded966999%99%
Active926796%97%

App opens per user are the same, and the steps after login convert normally. The login step is broken: 30% of 8.4 users who opened the app ended up logged out, versus 3% on 8.3. As in ps2, a multiplicative funnel can be attributed through logs: ln(0.70 / 0.97) = −0.326 explains all of ln(67 / 92) = −0.317 (the other steps net to slightly positive, +0.009). The investigation now has a place (Android 8.4) and a step (session refresh).

The server-side funnel also splits the client-side shortfall in two. Server data says about 67 of every 92 expected actives were really active: 2.4M × 67 / 92 ≈ 1.75M real actives on 8.4, so the real loss is about 0.65M. The client-side count was 1.45M, so another 0.30M (about 17% of really active 8.4 users) are missing from client events: a measurement loss on top of the real one.

7. Mix shift and Simpson's paradox

Many metrics are rates: conversion, retention, click-through. An overall rate is a weighted average of segment rates, weighted by each segment's share of the population. So it can change for two reasons: the segment rates changed (a rate effect), or the shares changed (a mix effect, from a mix shift). Confusing the two leads to fixing products that are not broken.

Worked example. A shop's checkout conversion fell from 3.0% to 2.66% week-over-week. By platform:

PlatformShare beforeRate beforeShare afterRate after
Desktop33.3%5.00%20.0%5.10%
Mobile66.7%2.00%80.0%2.05%
Overall100%3.00%100%2.66%

Both platforms improved, yet the total fell. Check: before, 0.333 × 5.0 + 0.667 × 2.0 = 1.667 + 1.333 = 3.00%; after, 0.2 × 5.1 + 0.8 × 2.05 = 1.02 + 1.64 = 2.66%. An exact decomposition of the −0.34 point change:

Mix effect = Σ (change in share × old rate) = (−0.133 × 5.0) + (+0.133 × 2.0) = −0.667 + 0.267 = −0.40 points.

Rate effect = Σ (new share × change in rate) = 0.2 × 0.10 + 0.8 × 0.05 = 0.02 + 0.04 = +0.06 points.

Total −0.40 + 0.06 = −0.34. The product's conversion got slightly better on both platforms; the overall rate fell because the traffic shifted to mobile, perhaps because a social-media campaign brought in many mobile visitors. The right response is not to "fix checkout" but to ask whether the extra mobile visitors are worth their acquisition cost, and to report conversion by platform from now on.

This is Simpson's paradox in its product form: a trend that holds in every group reverses when the groups are combined, because the groups' sizes differ in a way related to the outcome. The most famous real case is graduate admissions at the University of California, Berkeley, in fall 1973. Of 8,442 men who applied, 44% were admitted; of 4,321 women, 35%. The gap was too large to be chance. But department by department, the picture changed: in the six largest departments, women's admission rates were similar to or higher than men's in most of them. Women had applied disproportionately to the departments with low admission rates, and men to departments with high ones. The full data showed 4 of 85 departments significantly biased against women and 6 against men, and the 1975 analysis by Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell in Science found a small but statistically significant bias in favour of women once department was accounted for.
